cards.desc: Continuation of the descending thoracic aorta from the aortic hiatus at T12 to its bifurcation at L4, lying slightly to the left of the midline on the lumbar vertebral bodies.
cards.att: Begins at the aortic hiatus of the diaphragm at the lower border of T12, descends on the bodies of L1 to L4, and ends at L4 by dividing into the two common iliac arteries; the median sacral artery continues from the bifurcation.
cards.sup: Unpaired ventral branches: coeliac trunk (T12), superior mesenteric (L1), inferior mesenteric (L3). Paired lateral visceral: inferior phrenic, middle suprarenal, renal, gonadal. Paired parietal: four lumbar arteries.
cards.act: Arterial supply to the abdominal viscera and posterior abdominal wall, and through the common iliac arteries to the pelvis and lower limbs.
cards.rel: Anteriorly: coeliac plexus, body of pancreas, splenic vein, left renal vein and third part of duodenum. To the right lie the inferior vena cava and cisterna chyli; to the left, the left sympathetic trunk and duodenojejunal flexure.
cards.clin: Abdominal aortic aneurysm is usually infrarenal and presents as an expansile pulsatile mass above the umbilicus, with back pain and shock on rupture. The bifurcation lies at the supracristal plane (L4), the surface landmark used for palpation and for aortic compression.
cards.exam: Q. At which vertebral levels do the three unpaired ventral branches of the abdominal aorta arise? A. Coeliac trunk at T12, superior mesenteric artery at L1, inferior mesenteric artery at L3.

cards.desc: Retroperitoneal endocrine gland capping the upper pole of the kidney within the renal fascia, separated from the kidney by a septum of fat.
cards.att: The right gland is pyramidal and lies higher, behind the inferior vena cava and against the bare area of the liver; the left is semilunar and lies along the medial border of the upper kidney behind the lesser sac and pancreas. Each has a cortex (zona glomerulosa, fasciculata and reticularis) and a medulla of chromaffin cells.
cards.sup: Three arterial sources: superior suprarenal from the inferior phrenic artery, middle suprarenal from the aorta, inferior suprarenal from the renal artery. A single vein drains each gland: the short right vein directly into the inferior vena cava, the longer left vein into the left renal vein. Preganglionic sympathetic fibres from the greater splanchnic nerve synapse directly on medullary cells.
cards.act: Cortex secretes aldosterone, cortisol and androgens; the medulla secretes adrenaline and noradrenaline as a modified sympathetic ganglion.
cards.rel: The right gland lies behind the inferior vena cava and the bare area of the liver and in front of the diaphragm. The left lies behind the lesser sac and the body of the pancreas with the splenic artery, in front of the diaphragm and left crus.
cards.clin: The short right suprarenal vein draining straight into the inferior vena cava makes right adrenalectomy and right adrenal vein sampling technically hazardous. Bilateral haemorrhagic infarction in meningococcal septicaemia is the Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome. Phaeochromocytoma arises from the medulla.
cards.exam: Q. Where does each suprarenal vein drain? A. The right directly into the inferior vena cava, the left into the left renal vein.

cards.desc: Narrow blind-ended muscular tube of gut with abundant lymphoid tissue, arising from the posteromedial wall of the caecum about 2 cm below the ileocaecal junction.
cards.att: Base is fixed where the three taeniae coli converge on the caecum; the tip is mobile and lies retrocaecal (commonest), pelvic, subcaecal, pre-ileal or post-ileal. Suspended by the mesoappendix.
cards.sup: Appendicular artery, a branch of the ileocolic artery, running in the free edge of the mesoappendix. Veins drain to the superior mesenteric vein. Lymph to ileocolic nodes. Visceral afferents accompany sympathetics to T10.
cards.act: Gut-associated lymphoid tissue; no essential digestive function.
cards.rel: Base lies deep to McBurney's point, at the junction of the lateral and middle thirds of the line from the right anterior superior iliac spine to the umbilicus. A retrocaecal appendix lies against the iliacus and psoas major.
cards.clin: Appendicitis pain begins periumbilically (visceral, T10) and shifts to the right iliac fossa when the parietal peritoneum is irritated. A retrocaecal appendix gives a positive psoas sign; a pelvic appendix gives a positive obturator sign and tenderness on rectal examination. The appendicular artery is an end artery, so gangrene and perforation follow quickly.
cards.exam: Q. How is the base of the appendix found at operation? A. By tracing the taeniae coli of the caecum to their convergence.

cards.desc: First unpaired ventral branch of the abdominal aorta, arising at the level of T12 just below the aortic hiatus and dividing after about 1.5 cm into three branches.
cards.att: Arises from the front of the abdominal aorta at the T12 to L1 level, passes forwards and slightly to the right above the pancreas, and ends by trifurcating behind the omental bursa.
cards.sup: Left gastric, splenic and common hepatic arteries.
cards.act: Supplies the foregut derivatives: abdominal oesophagus, stomach, duodenum as far as the major duodenal papilla, liver, gallbladder, pancreas and spleen.
cards.rel: Surrounded by the coeliac plexus and its two ganglia, overhung by the median arcuate ligament and the crura, with the omental bursa and lesser omentum in front and the splenic vein and pancreas below.
cards.clin: Median arcuate ligament (Dunbar) syndrome: compression by a low-lying ligament causes postprandial epigastric pain, weight loss and an epigastric bruit. Slow coeliac occlusion is tolerated because the pancreaticoduodenal arcade connects it with the superior mesenteric artery.
cards.exam: Q. Name the three branches of the coeliac artery and the gut region it supplies. A. Left gastric, splenic and common hepatic arteries; the foregut.

cards.desc: Short wide artery, about 1.5 cm long, arising from the front of the abdominal aorta at T12 and trifurcating into the left gastric, splenic and common hepatic arteries.
cards.att: Arises immediately below the aortic hiatus at the T12 to L1 level between the crura of the diaphragm, runs forwards over the upper border of the pancreas, and ends by dividing into its three branches.
cards.sup: Left gastric artery (smallest), splenic artery (largest) and common hepatic artery; it may also give an inferior phrenic or a dorsal pancreatic branch.
cards.act: Carries the arterial supply of all foregut derivatives, with pain from these organs referred to the epigastrium.
cards.rel: Lies behind the omental bursa and the peritoneum of the lesser sac, embedded in the coeliac plexus, with the caudate lobe of the liver above and the body of the pancreas and splenic vein below.
cards.clin: Classical trifurcation is present in about 90 percent of people; hepatosplenic, gastrosplenic and hepatogastric variants and a common coeliacomesenteric trunk are recognised, and these variants must be defined on CT angiography before pancreatic or liver surgery.
cards.exam: Q. Which foregut structures does the coeliac trunk supply and where is their pain referred? A. Stomach, proximal duodenum, liver, gallbladder, pancreas and spleen, with pain referred to the epigastrium.

cards.desc: Branch of the coeliac trunk that runs to the right along the upper border of the pancreas towards the free edge of the lesser omentum.
cards.att: Arises from the coeliac trunk, passes forwards and to the right along the superior border of the head of the pancreas, and ends near the upper border of the first part of the duodenum by giving off the gastroduodenal artery and continuing as the hepatic artery proper.
cards.sup: Gastroduodenal artery and hepatic artery proper; the right gastric artery arises from one or the other.
cards.act: Supplies the liver, gallbladder, stomach, duodenum and part of the pancreas.
cards.rel: Forms the upper border of the epiploic foramen region as it enters the lesser omentum, lying anterior to the portal vein and to the left of the bile duct; the coeliac plexus surrounds its origin and the omental bursa lies behind.
cards.clin: Its gastroduodenal branch lies behind the first part of the duodenum and is eroded by a posterior duodenal ulcer, causing massive haematemesis. A replaced or accessory right hepatic artery from the superior mesenteric artery occurs in about one in five people and must be identified before pancreaticoduodenectomy.
cards.exam: Q. Which branch of the common hepatic artery lies behind the first part of the duodenum? A. The gastroduodenal artery.

cards.desc: Extrahepatic bile duct about 3 cm long, formed at the porta hepatis by union of the right and left hepatic ducts.
cards.att: Formed in the right end of the porta hepatis anterior to the right branch of the portal vein, descends in the free edge of the lesser omentum, and is joined on its right side by the cystic duct to form the bile duct (common bile duct).
cards.sup: Arterial supply from the cystic artery and the right hepatic artery, through a fine axial plexus running at the 3 o'clock and 9 o'clock positions. Lymph to the cystic and hilar nodes.
cards.act: Conveys bile from both hepatic ducts towards the bile duct and duodenum.
cards.rel: Lies to the right of the hepatic artery and anterior to the portal vein in the hepatoduodenal ligament. It forms the medial boundary of the cystohepatic triangle of Calot.
cards.clin: Mirizzi syndrome is obstruction of the common hepatic duct by a stone impacted in the cystic duct or Hartmann's pouch. The duct is at risk of injury during laparoscopic cholecystectomy when it is mistaken for the cystic duct, hence the critical view of safety.
cards.exam: Q. What forms the common hepatic duct and what does it become? A. Union of the right and left hepatic ducts; it becomes the bile duct after receiving the cystic duct.

cards.desc: Short duct, 3 to 4 cm long, running from the neck of the gallbladder to join the common hepatic duct and form the bile duct.
cards.att: Begins at the neck of the gallbladder, passes backwards, downwards and to the left in the free edge of the lesser omentum, and joins the right side of the common hepatic duct. Its mucosa is thrown into the spiral fold (valve of Heister).
cards.sup: Cystic artery, usually from the right hepatic artery. Lymph drains to the cystic node (of Lund) at the neck of the gallbladder.
cards.act: Conducts bile both into and out of the gallbladder; the spiral fold keeps the lumen patent.
cards.rel: Forms the lower boundary of the cystohepatic triangle of Calot, bounded also by the common hepatic duct medially and the inferior surface of the liver above. The cystic artery lies within this triangle.
cards.clin: Impaction of a stone in the cystic duct causes biliary colic and, if it persists, acute cholecystitis or a mucocele. Correct identification of the cystic duct and cystic artery, and of nothing else, entering the gallbladder is the critical view of safety in laparoscopic cholecystectomy.
cards.exam: Q. Name the boundaries and contents of Calot's triangle. A. Cystic duct below, common hepatic duct medially, inferior surface of the liver above; it contains the cystic artery.

cards.desc: C-shaped first part of the small intestine, about 25 cm long, curving around the head of the pancreas from the pylorus to the duodenojejunal flexure.
cards.att: Four parts: superior (first, about 5 cm, at L1, the proximal 2 cm intraperitoneal as the cap), descending (second, 7 to 10 cm, L1 to L3, receives the bile and pancreatic ducts), horizontal (third, 6 to 8 cm, at L3, crossed by the superior mesenteric vessels) and ascending (fourth, about 5 cm, ending at the duodenojejunal flexure at L2 left of the midline). Retroperitoneal except the cap.
cards.sup: Superior pancreaticoduodenal artery from the gastroduodenal (foregut) and inferior pancreaticoduodenal from the superior mesenteric artery (midgut), meeting at the major duodenal papilla. Veins to the portal and superior mesenteric veins. Nerves from the vagus and the greater and lesser splanchnic nerves via the coeliac and superior mesenteric plexuses.
cards.act: Receives chyme, bile and pancreatic juice; neutralises acid and begins the main phase of digestion.
cards.rel: The first part has the quadrate lobe of the liver and the gallbladder in front and above, and behind it the bile duct, gastroduodenal artery, portal vein and inferior vena cava. The second part lies on the hilum of the right kidney and the right renal vessels and is crossed anteriorly by the transverse colon and its mesocolon. The third part is crossed anteriorly by the superior mesenteric vessels and the root of the mesentery, and lies on the inferior vena cava and aorta.
cards.clin: Posterior duodenal ulcers erode the gastroduodenal artery and cause massive haematemesis; anterior ulcers perforate into the peritoneal cavity. The duodenojejunal flexure is suspended by the suspensory muscle of the duodenum (ligament of Treitz), the landmark separating upper from lower gastrointestinal bleeding.
cards.exam: Q. Which artery is eroded by a posterior duodenal ulcer? A. The gastroduodenal artery.

cards.desc: Largest and most superficial of the three flat muscles of the anterolateral abdominal wall, its fibres running downwards and forwards like hands in pockets.
cards.att: Origin from the outer surfaces and lower borders of the lower eight ribs (5 to 12) by fleshy digitations interdigitating with serratus anterior and latissimus dorsi. Inserts into the anterior half of the outer lip of the iliac crest, the pubic tubercle and pubic crest, and through a broad aponeurosis into the linea alba.
cards.sup: Anterior rami of T7 to T12 (thoracoabdominal nerves T7 to T11 and the subcostal nerve T12).
cards.act: Compresses the abdominal contents and raises intra-abdominal pressure; flexes the trunk; acting on one side it turns the trunk to the opposite side.
cards.rel: Superficial to internal oblique; its aponeurosis forms the anterior wall of the rectus sheath throughout. Its lower free border rolls back on itself between the anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic tubercle to form the inguinal ligament, and is deficient above the pubic crest as the superficial inguinal ring.
cards.clin: Its aponeurosis provides the inguinal ligament, lacunar ligament, superficial inguinal ring and the anterior wall of the inguinal canal, and is the layer reinforced in Bassini and Lichtenstein hernia repair. Splitting the muscle along its fibres is the first step of the grid-iron (McBurney) appendicectomy incision.
cards.exam: Q. Which structures are formed by the external oblique aponeurosis? A. The inguinal ligament, lacunar ligament, pectineal ligament, superficial inguinal ring and the anterior wall of the rectus sheath and inguinal canal.

cards.desc: The largest and lowest lumbar vertebra, sitting on the sacral base and forming the lumbosacral junction.
cards.att: Body is the largest of the vertebrae and wedge-shaped, deeper in front than behind; transverse processes are thick, conical and arise from the whole pedicle and the back of the body. Articulates with L4 above and with the sacrum below through the L5/S1 disc and paired zygapophysial joints.
cards.sup: Segmental supply from lumbar arteries and the iliolumbar artery; venous drainage to the internal and external vertebral venous plexuses.
cards.rel: The iliolumbar ligament runs from the tip of the transverse process to the iliac crest. The L5 nerve root passes below its pedicle; the sympathetic trunk, common iliac vessels and the median sacral vessels lie on the front of the body.
cards.clin: Commonest site of spondylolysis (pars interarticularis defect) and of spondylolisthesis of L5 on S1, producing a palpable step above the sacrum. The wedge shape of the body and disc creates the lumbosacral angle.
cards.exam: Q. At which vertebral level is spondylolisthesis most common? A. L5 on S1, usually through a pars interarticularis defect of L5.

cards.desc: The uppermost lumbar vertebra, at the thoracolumbar junction, with the smallest body and shortest transverse processes of the lumbar series.
cards.att: Kidney-shaped body, short thick pedicles, hatchet-shaped spinous process, triangular vertebral foramen; superior articular facets face posteromedially. Articulates with T12 above and L2 below.
cards.sup: First lumbar arteries from the abdominal aorta; drainage to lumbar veins and the vertebral venous plexuses.
cards.rel: The transpyloric plane crosses the lower border of the body. The right crus of the diaphragm arises from L1 to L3, the left from L1 to L2. The coeliac trunk arises at the upper border and the superior mesenteric artery at the lower border of L1.
cards.clin: The spinal cord ends (conus medullaris) at the L1/L2 disc in the adult, so lumbar puncture is performed below this level. The thoracolumbar junction is the commonest site of burst fracture in a fall from height.
cards.exam: Q. Which structures lie in the transpyloric plane at the lower border of L1? A. Pylorus, neck of pancreas, hila of the kidneys, origin of the superior mesenteric artery, and the ninth costal cartilages.

cards.desc: The fourth lumbar vertebra, the key surface landmark of the lumbar spine because the highest points of the iliac crests lie at its level.
cards.att: Typical lumbar form: large kidney-shaped body, hatchet-shaped spine, mamillary and accessory processes. Articulates with L3 above and L5 below at the discs and zygapophysial joints.
cards.sup: Fourth lumbar arteries from the abdominal aorta; internal and external vertebral venous plexuses.
cards.rel: The abdominal aorta bifurcates into the common iliac arteries at the lower border of L4, a little to the left of the midline. Psoas major and quadratus lumborum arise alongside the body and transverse process.
cards.clin: The supracristal (intercristal, Tuffier) plane joining the highest points of the iliac crests crosses the L4 spinous process or the L4/L5 interspace, the standard landmark for lumbar puncture and spinal anaesthesia in the adult.
cards.exam: Q. Where does the abdominal aorta bifurcate? A. At the lower border of the fourth lumbar vertebra, on the supracristal plane.

cards.desc: Pear-shaped sac of about 50 mL capacity lying in a fossa on the inferior surface of the right lobe of the liver, on the line separating the right and left functional lobes.
cards.att: Has a fundus, body and neck. The fundus projects beyond the inferior border of the liver at the tip of the ninth costal cartilage, where the lateral border of the right rectus abdominis crosses the costal margin. The neck narrows into the cystic duct and often bears a posteromedial dilatation, Hartmann's pouch. Its upper surface is attached to the liver, the rest covered by peritoneum.
cards.sup: Cystic artery from the right hepatic artery in Calot's triangle. Cystic veins drain into the portal vein and directly into the liver bed. Lymph to the cystic node of Lund, then hepatic and coeliac nodes. Parasympathetic supply from the vagus; sympathetic and visceral afferent fibres from T7 to T9 via the coeliac plexus.
cards.act: Stores and concentrates bile, and expels it into the duodenum under cholecystokinin stimulation.
cards.rel: The body lies on the transverse colon and the first and second parts of the duodenum. The fundus contacts the anterior abdominal wall at the tip of the ninth costal cartilage.
cards.clin: Murphy's sign is arrest of inspiration on palpation below the right costal margin in acute cholecystitis. Referred pain to the right shoulder tip (C3, C4) indicates diaphragmatic peritoneal irritation. A gallstone eroding into the duodenum can obstruct the terminal ileum (gallstone ileus).
cards.exam: Q. Where does the fundus of the gallbladder meet the anterior abdominal wall? A. At the tip of the ninth costal cartilage, where the lateral border of rectus abdominis crosses the costal margin.

cards.desc: Paired arteries running along the lesser curvature of the stomach between the layers of the lesser omentum, the left from the coeliac trunk and the right usually from the hepatic artery proper.
cards.att: The left gastric artery arises from the coeliac trunk, ascends to the cardia raising the gastropancreatic fold, then turns along the lesser curvature. The right gastric artery arises from the hepatic artery proper or common hepatic artery and runs to the left along the lesser curvature to anastomose with the left.
cards.sup: Oesophageal branches from the left gastric, gastric branches to both surfaces of the stomach; an accessory or replaced left hepatic artery may arise from the left gastric artery.
cards.act: Supply the lesser curvature and adjacent walls of the stomach and the abdominal oesophagus.
cards.rel: Both lie between the two layers of the lesser omentum along the lesser curvature, accompanied by the corresponding veins and by gastric lymph nodes.
cards.clin: The left gastric artery is the usual bleeding vessel in a chronic lesser curve gastric ulcer and is the target of angiographic embolisation. Its oesophageal branches accompany the veins that become oesophageal varices in portal hypertension.
cards.exam: Q. What is the commonest important arterial variant arising from the left gastric artery? A. An accessory or replaced left hepatic artery.

cards.desc: Paired veins accompanying the gastric arteries along the lesser curvature and draining directly into the hepatic portal vein.
cards.att: The left gastric (coronary) vein runs along the lesser curvature to the cardia, then turns backwards and to the right to enter the portal vein. The right gastric vein runs to the right along the lesser curvature and joins the portal vein above the pylorus.
cards.sup: The left gastric vein receives oesophageal tributaries; the right gastric vein receives the prepyloric vein of Mayo.
cards.act: Drain the lesser curvature of the stomach and the lower oesophagus into the portal system.
cards.rel: Both lie in the lesser omentum beside the corresponding arteries; the left gastric vein crosses behind or in front of the hepatic artery proper to reach the portal vein.
cards.clin: Oesophageal tributaries of the left gastric vein anastomose with oesophageal tributaries of the azygos vein; in portal hypertension this becomes oesophageal varices, the most lethal portosystemic shunt. The prepyloric vein of Mayo identifies the pylorus at operation.
cards.exam: Q. Which portosystemic anastomosis involves the left gastric vein? A. Its oesophageal tributaries with the oesophageal tributaries of the azygos vein, at the lower end of the oesophagus.

cards.desc: Continuation of the common hepatic artery beyond the origin of the gastroduodenal artery, ascending in the free edge of the lesser omentum to the porta hepatis.
cards.att: Begins where the common hepatic artery gives off the gastroduodenal artery, ascends in the hepatoduodenal ligament, and divides at or just below the porta hepatis into the right and left hepatic arteries.
cards.sup: Right and left hepatic arteries; the right hepatic gives the cystic artery, and the right gastric artery often arises from the proper hepatic.
cards.act: Delivers about a quarter of hepatic blood flow and roughly half the liver's oxygen, and is the arterial supply of the gallbladder and of the intrahepatic and upper extrahepatic bile ducts.
cards.rel: In the free edge of the lesser omentum it lies to the left of the bile duct and anterior to the portal vein; these three form the anterior boundary of the epiploic foramen.
cards.clin: The cystic artery is sought in the cystohepatic triangle of Calot, bounded by the cystic duct, the common hepatic duct and the inferior surface of the liver; misidentification of structures here is the cause of bile duct injury at cholecystectomy. Hepatic artery thrombosis after liver transplantation causes ischaemic biliary strictures because the ducts have no other arterial supply.
cards.exam: Q. What are the contents of the free edge of the lesser omentum and their arrangement? A. Hepatic artery proper on the left, bile duct on the right, portal vein behind both.

cards.desc: Most superficial and lateral of the thenar muscles, lying directly under the skin of the thenar eminence.
cards.att: Origin: flexor retinaculum, tubercle of the scaphoid and tubercle of the trapezium. Insertion: lateral side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the thumb, with a slip to the extensor expansion.
cards.sup: Recurrent (muscular) branch of the median nerve (C8, T1).
cards.act: Abducts the thumb at the carpometacarpal and metacarpophalangeal joints, moving it anteriorly at right angles to the palm.
cards.rel: Superficial to opponens pollicis and the superficial head of flexor pollicis brevis; the recurrent branch of the median nerve enters its deep surface.
cards.clin: The muscle tested in carpal tunnel syndrome: the patient abducts the thumb vertically against resistance with the hand flat. Thenar wasting with loss of palmar abduction is the classic median nerve sign, and it is the muscle used for opponensplasty assessment.
cards.exam: Q. Which single muscle best tests the median nerve in the hand? A. Abductor pollicis brevis, tested by palmar abduction of the thumb.

cards.desc: Deep muscle of the posterior forearm whose tendon emerges between the superficial extensors to form the lateral border of the anatomical snuffbox.
cards.att: Origin: posterior surface of the ulna below anconeus, the interosseous membrane and the posterior surface of the radius distal to supinator. Insertion: lateral side of the base of the first metacarpal, often with slips to the trapezium and abductor pollicis brevis.
cards.sup: Posterior interosseous nerve (C7, C8).
cards.act: Abducts and extends the thumb at the carpometacarpal joint; assists abduction of the wrist.
cards.rel: With extensor pollicis brevis it winds round the lateral border of the radius superficial to the radial extensors of the wrist, forming the outcropping muscles; both tendons occupy the first extensor compartment and form the anterior boundary of the anatomical snuffbox.
cards.clin: Stenosing tenosynovitis of its tendon with extensor pollicis brevis in the first extensor compartment is de Quervain's disease, positive on Finkelstein's test. The tendon is a graft source for basal thumb joint reconstruction.
cards.exam: Q. Which tendons occupy the first extensor compartment of the wrist? A. Abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis.

cards.desc: The thick multipennate middle portion of deltoid arising from the acromion, the only truly multipennate part of the muscle.
cards.att: Origin: lateral margin and superior surface of the acromion. Insertion: deltoid tuberosity on the lateral surface of the humerus, in common with the other parts.
cards.sup: Axillary nerve (C5, C6).
cards.act: The chief abductor of the arm from about 15 to 90 degrees, after supraspinatus initiates abduction.
cards.rel: Overlies the subacromial bursa, the supraspinatus tendon and the greater tubercle; the axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral vessels run on its deep surface about 5 to 7 cm below the acromion.
cards.clin: Paralysis after surgical neck fracture of the humerus or shoulder dislocation causes loss of abduction and a flattened shoulder contour with loss of sensation over the regimental badge area. The multipennate structure gives power at the cost of range.
cards.exam: Q. Why is the acromial part of deltoid multipennate? A. To generate the power needed to abduct the arm against gravity beyond 15 degrees.

cards.desc: Main artery of the axilla, continuing the subclavian artery and supplying the shoulder region and upper limb.
cards.att: Begins as the continuation of the subclavian artery at the outer border of the first rib and ends at the lower border of teres major, where it becomes the brachial artery; pectoralis minor crossing it divides it into three parts.
cards.sup: First part: superior thoracic artery. Second part: thoraco-acromial and lateral thoracic arteries. Third part: subscapular, anterior circumflex humeral and posterior circumflex humeral arteries, giving one, two and three branches from the three parts.
cards.act: Supplies the shoulder girdle, the walls and contents of the axilla, the lateral part of the breast, and through its continuation the whole upper limb.
cards.rel: Enclosed with the brachial plexus in the axillary sheath; the cords of the plexus are named from their relation to its second part. The axillary vein lies medial to it throughout, and the axillary nerve and radial nerve lie behind its third part.
cards.clin: At risk in anterior shoulder dislocation and proximal humeral fracture, and may be compressed against the humeral head. It can be ligated between the thyrocervical trunk and the subscapular artery because the scapular anastomosis restores flow, but ligation distal to the subscapular origin threatens the limb.
cards.exam: Q. What divides the axillary artery into its three parts? A. Pectoralis minor: the first part is proximal to it, the second behind it, the third distal to it.

cards.desc: Large vein of the axilla draining the whole upper limb, lying medial to the axillary artery.
cards.att: Formed at the lower border of teres major by the union of the brachial venae comitantes with the basilic vein, ascends medial and slightly anterior to the axillary artery, and becomes the subclavian vein at the outer border of the first rib.
cards.sup: Receives tributaries corresponding to the branches of the axillary artery, together with the cephalic vein, which pierces the clavipectoral fascia to join it, and the thoraco-epigastric vein.
cards.rel: Lies medial to the axillary artery and partly overlaps it; the medial cord of the brachial plexus, the ulnar nerve and the medial cutaneous nerve of the forearm lie between the vein and the artery. The lateral (humeral) and apical groups of axillary lymph nodes lie along it.
cards.clin: Used for infraclavicular central venous access; its walls are held open by surrounding fascia, so a tear can draw in air and cause air embolism. Effort thrombosis (Paget-Schroetter syndrome) affects the axillary and subclavian veins, and dissection along the vein in axillary clearance risks lymphoedema.
cards.exam: Q. Where does the axillary vein begin and end? A. At the lower border of teres major, from the brachial veins and basilic vein, ending at the outer border of the first rib as the subclavian vein.

cards.desc: Large superficial vein on the medial side of the forearm and arm that becomes a deep vein in the arm.
cards.att: Begins at the ulnar end of the dorsal venous network, ascends on the ulnar side of the front of the forearm, passes in front of the medial epicondyle, and pierces the deep fascia at about the middle of the arm to run with the brachial artery and join the brachial veins at the lower border of teres major as the axillary vein.
cards.sup: Receives the median cubital vein and often the median vein of the forearm at the elbow, together with tributaries from the medial forearm and arm.
cards.rel: Accompanied by the medial cutaneous nerve of the forearm below the elbow and by branches of the same nerve in the arm; after piercing the deep fascia it lies medial to the brachial artery.
cards.clin: The vein of choice for peripherally inserted central catheters because of its straight course into the axillary vein, and it is transposed and anastomosed to the brachial artery to create a dialysis fistula when forearm vessels have failed.
cards.exam: Q. Where does the basilic vein pierce the deep fascia? A. At about the middle of the arm, at the hiatus basilicus in the medial intermuscular septum.

cards.desc: Main artery of the arm, the continuation of the axillary artery on the front of the arm.
cards.att: Begins at the lower border of teres major, descends on the medial side of the arm and then on brachialis in front of the humerus, and ends in the cubital fossa at the level of the neck of the radius by dividing into the radial and ulnar arteries.
cards.sup: Profunda brachii (deep brachial), superior ulnar collateral, inferior ulnar collateral, the nutrient artery to the humerus and muscular branches; terminates as the radial and ulnar arteries.
cards.act: Supplies the flexor and extensor compartments of the arm, the humerus and the elbow, and carries the entire blood supply of the forearm and hand.
cards.rel: The median nerve crosses it from lateral to medial in the middle of the arm. In the cubital fossa it lies between the median nerve medially and the tendon of biceps laterally, covered by the bicipital aponeurosis; the ulnar nerve leaves it in the upper arm to pass behind the medial epicondyle.
cards.clin: The artery used for blood pressure measurement and the brachial pulse, felt medial to the biceps tendon. In supracondylar fracture of the humerus, injury or spasm produces forearm ischaemia and Volkmann ischaemic contracture; pain on passive extension of the fingers with a weak radial pulse is the warning sign.
cards.exam: Q. At what level does the brachial artery divide, and into what? A. At the level of the neck of the radius in the cubital fossa, into the radial and ulnar arteries.

cards.desc: Flat muscle on the lower half of the front of the humerus, lying deep to biceps brachii and crossing only the elbow joint.
cards.att: Origin: lower half of the anterior surface of the humerus and the adjacent medial and lateral intermuscular septa. Insertion: tuberosity and anterior surface of the coronoid process of the ulna.
cards.sup: Musculocutaneous nerve (C5, C6); the lateral part receives a twig from the radial nerve (C7).
cards.act: The main flexor of the elbow, working in all positions of the forearm because it inserts on the ulna and is unaffected by pronation and supination.
cards.rel: Forms the floor of the cubital fossa with supinator; the median nerve and brachial artery lie on it medially, the radial nerve between it and brachioradialis laterally; biceps brachii lies superficial.
cards.clin: Direct trauma to the muscle is a common cause of myositis ossificans at the elbow. Supracondylar fracture fragments may pierce it and injure the underlying brachial artery and median nerve, and it is the muscle interposed in anterior elbow dislocation.
cards.exam: Q. Why is brachialis called the workhorse flexor of the elbow? A. Because it inserts on the ulna and therefore flexes the elbow with equal power in supination, pronation and midprone positions.

cards.desc: Most superficial and lateral muscle of the forearm, forming the prominent lateral border of the cubital fossa.
cards.att: Origin: upper two-thirds of the lateral supracondylar ridge of the humerus and the anterior surface of the lateral intermuscular septum. Insertion: lateral side of the base of the styloid process of the radius.
cards.sup: Radial nerve (C5, C6, C7), in the arm before the nerve divides.
cards.act: Flexes the elbow, most powerfully with the forearm in the midprone position; it is a shunt muscle rather than a true supinator or pronator.
cards.rel: Forms the lateral boundary of the cubital fossa; the radial nerve and radial artery lie deep to it in the forearm, the artery emerging at its medial border where the radial pulse is felt.
cards.clin: An anomaly among flexors: it flexes the elbow yet is supplied by the radial nerve. It is paralysed with the wrist extensors when the radial nerve is injured in the spiral groove, but spared in a posterior interosseous nerve lesion, so preserved brachioradialis localises the lesion below the elbow; the brachioradialis jerk tests C5 and C6.
cards.exam: Q. In which position of the forearm does brachioradialis act most powerfully, and what nerve supplies it? A. The midprone position, supplied by the radial nerve (C5, C6, C7).

cards.desc: Large superficial vein on the lateral side of the forearm and arm, ending in the deltopectoral groove.
cards.att: Begins at the radial end of the dorsal venous network, winds round the radial border of the forearm on to its front, ascends lateral to biceps in the arm, runs in the deltopectoral groove between deltoid and pectoralis major, and pierces the clavipectoral fascia to end in the axillary vein.
cards.sup: Receives the accessory cephalic vein in the forearm and gives off the median cubital vein at the elbow; drains the radial side of the hand, forearm and arm.
cards.rel: Lies in the superficial fascia throughout; in the deltopectoral groove it accompanies the deltoid branch of the thoraco-acromial artery and lies within the deltopectoral triangle below the clavicle.
cards.clin: Approached in the deltopectoral groove for venous cutdown and for the insertion of cardiac pacemaker leads. At the wrist it is anastomosed to the radial artery to form the radiocephalic (Brescia-Cimino) dialysis fistula.
cards.exam: Q. What structure does the cephalic vein pierce to reach the axillary vein? A. The clavipectoral fascia.

cards.desc: Subcutaneous S-shaped long bone lying horizontally at the root of the neck, the only bony strut connecting the upper limb to the axial skeleton.
cards.att: Medial two-thirds are convex forwards and rounded, the lateral third is concave forwards and flattened. It articulates medially at the sternoclavicular joint and laterally at the acromioclavicular joint. Landmarks: subclavian groove on the inferior surface, conoid tubercle and trapezoid ridge laterally, and the impression for the costoclavicular ligament medially. Pectoralis major, deltoid, sternocleidomastoid, trapezius, subclavius and sternohyoid attach to it.
cards.act: Acts as a strut holding the shoulder away from the trunk and transmits force from the upper limb to the axial skeleton.
cards.rel: The subclavian vessels and the trunks of the brachial plexus pass behind its middle third, separated from it by subclavius and the clavipectoral fascia. The apex of the lung lies behind its medial end.
cards.clin: It is the first bone to ossify (fifth to sixth intrauterine week) and the last epiphysis in the body to fuse (sternal end, about 25 years), which makes it useful for age estimation. Fracture is commonest at the junction of the middle and lateral thirds: the lateral fragment is pulled down by the weight of the limb and the medial fragment up by sternocleidomastoid.
cards.exam: Q. Where does the clavicle usually fracture and how do the fragments displace? A. At the junction of the middle and lateral thirds; the medial fragment is pulled up by sternocleidomastoid and the lateral fragment drops with the weight of the limb.

cards.desc: Slender muscle of the anterior compartment of the arm running from the coracoid process to the middle of the medial surface of the humerus.
cards.att: Origin: tip of the coracoid process of the scapula, by a tendon common with the short head of biceps brachii. Insertion: middle third of the medial surface and border of the humerus.
cards.sup: Musculocutaneous nerve (C5, C6, C7), which pierces the muscle.
cards.act: Flexes and adducts the arm at the shoulder; helps stabilise the humeral head.
cards.rel: Pierced by the musculocutaneous nerve; forms the lateral wall of the axilla with the humerus and biceps; the axillary and brachial arteries and the median and ulnar nerves lie medial to it.
cards.clin: Called the perforated muscle because the musculocutaneous nerve passes through it; the nerve can be entrapped there causing weak elbow flexion and numbness on the lateral forearm. It is a landmark for locating the neurovascular bundle in the arm.
cards.exam: Q. Which nerve pierces coracobrachialis? A. The musculocutaneous nerve (C5, C6, C7).

cards.desc: Largest branch of the brachial artery, accompanying the radial nerve behind the shaft of the humerus.
cards.att: Arises from the brachial artery just below the lower border of teres major, passes with the radial nerve through the triangular interval into the spiral (radial) groove between the medial and lateral heads of triceps, and divides into radial collateral and middle collateral branches.
cards.sup: Radial collateral artery, which pierces the lateral intermuscular septum with the radial nerve to meet the radial recurrent artery, the middle collateral artery, which descends behind the lateral epicondyle to meet the interosseous recurrent artery, a nutrient branch to the humerus, and branches to triceps and deltoid.
cards.act: Supplies triceps and the posterior compartment of the arm, the humeral shaft, and contributes to the arterial anastomosis round the elbow.
cards.rel: Lies in the spiral groove directly against the shaft of the humerus with the radial nerve, between the medial and lateral heads of triceps.
cards.clin: Injured with the radial nerve in mid-shaft (spiral groove) fractures of the humerus, which classically produce wrist drop with preserved elbow extension. Its collateral branches keep the forearm perfused if the brachial artery is occluded at the elbow.
cards.exam: Q. Which nerve accompanies the profunda brachii artery and where? A. The radial nerve, in the spiral (radial) groove of the humerus.

cards.desc: Arterial arch across the bases of the metacarpals in the deepest plane of the palm.
cards.att: Formed mainly by the terminal part of the radial artery, which enters the palm between the two heads of the first dorsal interosseous and then between the heads of adductor pollicis, and is completed on the ulnar side by the deep branch of the ulnar artery; it lies on the interossei and the bases of the metacarpals.
cards.sup: Three palmar metacarpal arteries, three perforating branches that pass back to the dorsal metacarpal arteries, and recurrent branches to the carpal arch; the princeps pollicis and radialis indicis arise from the radial artery as the arch is formed.
cards.act: Supplies the deep structures of the palm and, through the palmar metacarpal arteries, reinforces the digital supply from the superficial arch.
cards.rel: Lies deep to the long flexor tendons, the lumbricals and adductor pollicis, and is accompanied by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve. It lies about a finger's breadth proximal to the superficial palmar arch.
cards.clin: The Allen test confirms that both radial and ulnar arteries fill the arches before radial artery cannulation or radial forearm flap harvest. A penetrating palmar wound bleeds from both ends of the arch, so ligation of one feeding artery alone does not control it.
cards.exam: Q. Which artery mainly forms the deep palmar arch? A. The radial artery, completed by the deep branch of the ulnar artery.

cards.desc: The upper fibres of trapezius, descending from the skull and ligamentum nuchae to the lateral clavicle.
cards.att: Origin: medial third of the superior nuchal line, external occipital protuberance and the ligamentum nuchae down to the C7 spine. Insertion: posterior border of the lateral third of the clavicle.
cards.sup: Accessory nerve (CN XI) for motor supply, with proprioceptive fibres from the ventral rami of C3 and C4.
cards.act: Elevates the scapula and, with the ascending part and serratus anterior, rotates the glenoid cavity upwards; extends the head and neck when the scapula is fixed.
cards.rel: Its anterior border forms the posterior boundary of the posterior triangle of the neck. The accessory nerve crosses the triangle obliquely and passes deep to that border about 5 cm above the clavicle, reaching the deep surface of the muscle.
cards.clin: The accessory nerve is vulnerable during lymph node biopsy in the posterior triangle; injury causes shoulder droop, weak shrugging and inability to abduct the arm fully above the head. Shoulder shrug against resistance is the standard bedside test.
cards.exam: Q. Where is the accessory nerve most at risk of surgical injury? A. In the posterior triangle of the neck, along the anterior border of the descending part of trapezius.

cards.desc: Superficial extensor of the posterior forearm lying deep to extensor carpi radialis longus, arising from the common extensor origin.
cards.att: Origin: lateral epicondyle of the humerus by the common extensor tendon, and the adjacent intermuscular septa and antebrachial fascia. Insertion: dorsal surface of the base of the third metacarpal.
cards.sup: Deep branch of the radial nerve (C7, C8), given off before or as it becomes the posterior interosseous nerve.
cards.act: Extends the wrist and, with extensor carpi radialis longus and flexor carpi radialis, abducts it (radial deviation); acting together with extensor carpi ulnaris it produces pure wrist extension, essential for making a strong fist by stabilising the wrist in extension.
cards.rel: Lies deep to extensor carpi radialis longus and is crossed distally by abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis; both radial extensor tendons occupy the second extensor compartment under the extensor retinaculum.
cards.clin: Its origin from the common extensor tendon is the site of lateral epicondylitis (tennis elbow), and the deep surface of its origin is what is released or debrided surgically.
cards.exam: Q. Which muscle origin is chiefly involved in tennis elbow? A. The origin of extensor carpi radialis brevis from the common extensor tendon on the lateral epicondyle.

cards.desc: Long radial wrist extensor arising above the lateral epicondyle, lying between brachioradialis and extensor carpi radialis brevis.
cards.att: Origin: lower third of the lateral supracondylar ridge of the humerus and the lateral intermuscular septum. Insertion: dorsal surface of the base of the second metacarpal.
cards.sup: Radial nerve (C6, C7), directly, before the nerve divides into superficial and deep branches.
cards.act: Extends and abducts (radially deviates) the wrist; weakly flexes the elbow.
cards.rel: With brachioradialis it forms the mobile wad of the lateral forearm; its tendon lies in the second extensor compartment with extensor carpi radialis brevis, crossed superficially by abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis.
cards.clin: Because it is supplied by the radial nerve trunk rather than the posterior interosseous nerve, wrist extension is partly preserved with radial deviation in posterior interosseous nerve palsy, so there is no true wrist drop. Its tendon is a standard donor for tendon transfer.
cards.exam: Q. Why is there no complete wrist drop in posterior interosseous nerve palsy? A. Extensor carpi radialis longus is supplied by the radial nerve proper and still extends the wrist, with radial deviation.

cards.desc: Most anterior muscle of the adductor group, forming the medial boundary of the femoral triangle.
cards.att: Origin: front of the body of the pubis in the angle between the crest and the symphysis, by a narrow tendon. Insertion: middle third of the linea aspera of the femur.
cards.sup: Obturator nerve, anterior division (L2, L3, L4).
cards.act: Adducts, flexes and medially rotates the thigh at the hip.
cards.rel: Its medial border forms the medial boundary of the femoral triangle, and it helps form the floor of the triangle with iliopsoas and pectineus; lower down it forms part of the posterior wall of the adductor canal with adductor magnus. Adductor brevis and the anterior division of the obturator nerve lie behind it.
cards.clin: Its narrow tendinous origin is the commonest site of adductor strain or groin pull in footballers. Chronic traction can produce ossification in the tendon, the rider bone of horse riders.
cards.exam: Q. What forms the medial boundary of the femoral triangle? A. The medial border of adductor longus.

cards.desc: Large triangular composite muscle forming the posterior wall of the adductor compartment, with an adductor part and a hamstring part.
cards.att: Origin: adductor part from the inferior pubic ramus and ramus of the ischium, hamstring part from the inferolateral part of the ischial tuberosity. Insertion: adductor part into the gluteal tuberosity, linea aspera and medial supracondylar line; hamstring part by a rounded tendon into the adductor tubercle of the medial femoral condyle.
cards.sup: Adductor part by the obturator nerve, posterior division (L2, L3, L4); hamstring part by the tibial division of the sciatic nerve (L4).
cards.act: Powerful adductor of the thigh; the adductor part also flexes and the hamstring part extends the hip.
cards.rel: Pierced by the four perforating arteries near the linea aspera. The osseoaponeurotic adductor hiatus between its aponeurotic insertion and the adductor tubercle transmits the femoral vessels into the popliteal fossa.
cards.clin: At the adductor hiatus the femoral artery becomes the popliteal artery, a fixed point where the vessel is tethered and vulnerable. The adductor tubercle is the palpable landmark for the medial collateral and medial patellofemoral ligaments and for measuring limb length.
cards.exam: Q. What is the dual nerve supply of adductor magnus? A. Obturator nerve to the adductor part and the tibial division of the sciatic nerve to the hamstring part.

cards.desc: Main artery of the anterior (extensor) compartment of the leg, running from the back of the knee to the front of the ankle.
cards.att: Arises as the smaller terminal branch of the popliteal artery at the lower border of popliteus, passes forwards above the upper border of the interosseous membrane into the anterior compartment, then descends on the anterior surface of the membrane and the lower tibia, and becomes the dorsalis pedis artery midway between the malleoli at the level of the ankle joint.
cards.sup: Anterior tibial recurrent, muscular branches, anterior medial malleolar and anterior lateral malleolar arteries.
cards.act: Supplies the extensor compartment muscles, the anterior part of the ankle and the skin over the front of the leg.
cards.rel: Accompanied by the deep fibular nerve, which crosses from lateral to anterior and then lies lateral to the artery in the lower leg; lies between tibialis anterior medially and extensor digitorum longus, then extensor hallucis longus, laterally; venae comitantes on either side.
cards.clin: Vulnerable in fractures of the upper tibia and in anterior compartment syndrome, where rising compartment pressure causes deep pain on passive plantarflexion, weak dorsiflexion, and numbness in the first web space; distal pulses may still be present.
cards.exam: Q. Where does the anterior tibial artery enter the anterior compartment of the leg? A. Through the gap above the upper border of the interosseous membrane.

cards.desc: The thickest and strongest tendon in the body, formed by the triceps surae and inserting on the heel.
cards.att: Formed by union of the tendons of the two heads of gastrocnemius and of soleus about the middle of the leg; the fibres spiral about ninety degrees as they descend and insert into the middle part of the posterior surface of the calcaneus.
cards.sup: Blood supply from branches of the posterior tibial and fibular arteries; sensory innervation from the tibial and sural nerves.
cards.act: Transmits the plantarflexion force of the triceps surae to the heel, giving the push off in walking, running and jumping.
cards.rel: The retrocalcaneal bursa lies between the tendon and the upper part of the posterior surface of the calcaneus, and a subcutaneous bursa lies behind it. The sural nerve and small saphenous vein lie along its lateral border; the tibial neurovascular bundle and deep flexor tendons lie deep and medial to it.
cards.clin: Ruptures typically 2 to 6 cm above the insertion, a relatively avascular watershed zone, with a palpable gap and a positive Simmonds or Thompson calf squeeze test. Its integrity is tested clinically by the ankle jerk (S1, S2).
cards.exam: Q. Why does the calcaneal tendon usually rupture 2 to 6 cm above its insertion? A. That segment is a relatively avascular watershed zone between its proximal and distal blood supply.

cards.desc: Largest and strongest tarsal bone, forming the heel and transmitting body weight to the ground behind the talus.
cards.att: Parts: body, calcaneal tuberosity with medial and lateral processes, sustentaculum tali, anterior process, and the fibular (peroneal) trochlea laterally. Articulates above with the talus by anterior, middle and posterior facets and in front with the cuboid. The calcaneal tendon inserts on the middle of the posterior surface; the plantar aponeurosis, abductor hallucis, flexor digitorum brevis and abductor digiti minimi arise from the tuberosity; the groove below sustentaculum tali carries the tendon of flexor hallucis longus.
cards.act: Transmits body weight to the ground, acts as the lever arm for the calf muscles and forms the posterior pillar of the lateral longitudinal arch.
cards.rel: The sinus tarsi and tarsal canal between calcaneus and talus hold the interosseous talocalcaneal ligament. Medially the tarsal tunnel structures cross it; the fibular tendons pass on either side of the fibular trochlea laterally.
cards.clin: A fall from a height causes a compression fracture of the calcaneus, often bilateral and associated with a burst fracture of the lumbar spine, and Böhler's angle is reduced. A calcaneal spur at the origin of the plantar aponeurosis is associated with plantar fasciitis, and the medial process is the usual site of heel pain.
cards.exam: Q. What injuries are typically associated with a calcaneal fracture from a fall on the heels? A. A fracture of the opposite calcaneus and a compression or burst fracture of the thoracolumbar spine.

cards.desc: Artery of the dorsum of the foot, the direct continuation of the anterior tibial artery.
cards.att: Begins at the ankle joint midway between the malleoli as the continuation of the anterior tibial artery, runs distally over the talus, navicular and intermediate cuneiform, and ends at the proximal end of the first intermetatarsal space by passing into the sole between the two heads of the first dorsal interosseous as the deep plantar artery, which completes the plantar arch.
cards.sup: Lateral tarsal, medial tarsal, arcuate (giving the second to fourth dorsal metatarsal arteries), first dorsal metatarsal and deep plantar arteries.
cards.act: Supplies the dorsum of the foot and contributes the deep plantar artery to the plantar arch of the sole.
cards.rel: Lies lateral to the tendon of extensor hallucis longus and medial to the tendon of extensor digitorum longus to the second toe, crossed distally by the tendon of extensor hallucis brevis; the deep fibular nerve lies on its lateral side; it is covered only by skin, fascia and the inferior extensor retinaculum.
cards.clin: Its pulse is felt just lateral to the extensor hallucis longus tendon on the dorsum and is a routine test of distal limb perfusion; it is congenitally absent or aberrant in a small minority of normal people, so absence alone does not prove arterial disease.
cards.exam: Q. Where do you palpate the dorsalis pedis pulse? A. On the dorsum of the foot, immediately lateral to the tendon of extensor hallucis longus, between the first and second metatarsal bases.

cards.desc: Muscle of the anterior compartment of the leg that extends the great toe, its tendon lying between tibialis anterior and extensor digitorum longus at the ankle.
cards.att: Origin: middle half of the medial surface of the fibula and the adjacent interosseous membrane. Insertion: dorsal surface of the base of the distal phalanx of the great toe.
cards.sup: Deep fibular nerve (L5, S1).
cards.act: Extends the great toe at the interphalangeal and metatarsophalangeal joints; assists dorsiflexion of the ankle and weak inversion of the foot.
cards.rel: Concealed above by tibialis anterior and extensor digitorum longus. At the ankle the anterior tibial artery and deep fibular nerve lie lateral to its tendon, and the dorsalis pedis pulse is felt immediately lateral to it on the dorsum.
cards.clin: Weakness of great toe extension is the classic single sign of an L5 root lesion from a prolapsed L4 to L5 disc. Its tendon is the landmark for palpating the dorsalis pedis pulse.
cards.exam: Q. Weakness of extensor hallucis longus indicates which root lesion? A. L5.

cards.desc: Main artery of the lower limb, running from the inguinal ligament to the adductor hiatus.
cards.att: Continuation of the external iliac artery behind the inguinal ligament at the mid-inguinal point, midway between the anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic symphysis; it passes through the femoral triangle and then the adductor canal, and becomes the popliteal artery at the adductor hiatus in adductor magnus.
cards.sup: Superficial epigastric, superficial circumflex iliac, superficial external pudendal, deep external pudendal, profunda femoris and descending genicular arteries.
cards.act: Supplies the lower limb and the lower anterior abdominal wall and external genitalia through its superficial branches.
cards.rel: In the femoral triangle it lies lateral to the femoral vein and medial to the femoral nerve, within the femoral sheath which does not contain the nerve; in the adductor canal it lies deep to sartorius with the saphenous nerve crossing it from lateral to medial and the nerve to vastus medialis laterally.
cards.clin: The femoral pulse is felt below the mid-inguinal point and is the standard puncture site for coronary and peripheral angiography; puncture above the inguinal ligament risks uncontrollable retroperitoneal haemorrhage. Remember the order from lateral to medial: nerve, artery, vein, empty space, lymphatics (NAVEL).
cards.exam: Q. What are the boundaries of the femoral triangle? A. Inguinal ligament above, medial border of sartorius laterally, medial border of adductor longus medially, with a floor of iliopsoas, pectineus and adductor longus.

cards.desc: Main deep vein of the thigh, continuing the popliteal vein up to the inguinal ligament.
cards.att: Begins as the continuation of the popliteal vein at the adductor hiatus, ascends through the adductor canal and femoral triangle within the femoral sheath, and becomes the external iliac vein at the inguinal ligament.
cards.sup: Receives the deep femoral vein, the great saphenous vein at the saphenofemoral junction, and the circumflex femoral veins.
cards.act: Carries the whole deep venous return of the lower limb.
cards.rel: Lies posterolateral to the artery at the adductor hiatus, posterior to it in mid-thigh, and medial to it at the inguinal ligament, where it occupies the intermediate compartment of the femoral sheath with the femoral canal medial to it.
cards.clin: Femoral venous puncture for central access is made about a centimetre medial to the femoral arterial pulse below the inguinal ligament. Thrombosis of the femoral vein is a proximal DVT with a high risk of pulmonary embolism, presenting with a swollen, tender, warm limb.
cards.exam: Q. What is the relation of the femoral vein to the femoral artery at the base of the femoral triangle? A. The vein lies medial to the artery.

cards.desc: Longest, heaviest and strongest bone of the body, forming the skeleton of the thigh between the hip and the knee.
cards.att: Upper end: head with the fovea for the ligament of the head, neck, greater and lesser trochanters, intertrochanteric line in front and intertrochanteric crest with the quadrate tubercle behind. Shaft: linea aspera with medial and lateral lips, gluteal tuberosity, pectineal line, popliteal surface. Lower end: medial and lateral condyles, epicondyles, adductor tubercle, intercondylar fossa and patellar surface. Articulates with the acetabulum above and with the tibia and patella below. The neck-shaft angle is about 125 degrees and the angle of anteversion about 15 degrees in the adult.
cards.sup: Retinacular branches of the medial and lateral circumflex femoral arteries, the medial being dominant, the artery of the ligament of the head, and nutrient arteries from the perforating branches of the profunda femoris artery.
cards.act: Transmits body weight from the hip bone to the tibia and acts as the lever for the muscles of the hip and knee.
cards.rel: The femoral vessels lie in front of the hip and pass through the adductor canal on its medial side; the sciatic nerve runs behind the ischium and the popliteal vessels lie on the popliteal surface. The profunda femoris artery and its perforating branches hug the linea aspera.
cards.clin: Fracture of the femoral neck in the elderly tears the retinacular vessels and leads to avascular necrosis of the head; the limb is short and laterally rotated. A shaft fracture can lose more than a litre of blood, and the ossification centre in the lower end, present at birth, is used medicolegally as a sign of maturity.
cards.exam: Q. Why is avascular necrosis common after an intracapsular fracture of the femoral neck? A. Because the retinacular branches of the medial circumflex femoral artery, the main supply to the head, run in the capsule and are torn.

cards.desc: Slender lateral bone of the leg, not weight bearing, giving attachment to muscles and forming the lateral malleolus of the ankle.
cards.att: Parts: head with an apex or styloid process, neck, triangular shaft with three borders and three surfaces, and the lateral malleolus with the malleolar fossa and a groove behind for the fibular tendons. Articulates with the lateral condyle of the tibia at the superior tibiofibular joint, with the tibia through the interosseous membrane and the inferior tibiofibular syndesmosis, and with the lateral surface of the talus at the ankle. Gives origin to the fibularis muscles laterally, extensor digitorum longus, extensor hallucis longus and fibularis tertius in front, and soleus, flexor hallucis longus and tibialis posterior behind; biceps femoris inserts on the head.
cards.act: Stabilises the ankle mortise, deepens the socket for the talus and provides muscle attachment; it transmits almost no body weight.
cards.rel: The common fibular nerve winds round the neck of the fibula against bone, between it and fibularis longus, before dividing into superficial and deep fibular nerves. The lateral malleolus reaches about 1 cm lower and lies more posterior than the medial malleolus.
cards.clin: Fracture of the neck or tight plaster at this level injures the common fibular nerve and causes foot drop with loss of sensation on the dorsum of the foot. In a Maisonneuve injury a proximal fibular fracture accompanies a medial ankle injury, so the whole fibula must be examined; the middle shaft is the standard donor for a vascularised bone graft.
cards.exam: Q. Which nerve is at risk in a fracture of the neck of the fibula, and what is the result? A. The common fibular nerve, producing foot drop with loss of dorsiflexion and eversion.

cards.desc: Superficial and longer muscle of the lateral compartment, whose tendon crosses the sole to reach the medial side of the foot.
cards.att: Origin: head and upper two thirds of the lateral surface of the fibula and the adjacent intermuscular septa. Insertion: lateral side of the base of the first metatarsal and of the medial cuneiform, after passing behind the lateral malleolus, below the fibular trochlea and through the groove on the cuboid.
cards.sup: Superficial fibular nerve (L5, S1).
cards.act: Everts the foot and plantarflexes the ankle; its sling across the sole supports the transverse and lateral longitudinal arches.
cards.rel: Covers fibularis brevis; the common fibular nerve divides deep to its upper attachment, between the muscle and the neck of the fibula. In the sole its tendon runs in a groove on the cuboid, held by the long plantar ligament, deep to all other structures.
cards.clin: The common fibular nerve is compressed against the fibular neck under this muscle by plaster casts, prolonged squatting or crossed legs, causing foot drop with loss of eversion. A sesamoid, the os peroneum, may lie in the tendon over the cuboid and fracture.
cards.exam: Q. Where is the common fibular nerve most often injured, and what is the deformity? A. Against the neck of the fibula, causing foot drop with loss of dorsiflexion and eversion.

cards.desc: Most lateral metatarsal, recognised by the prominent tuberosity projecting backwards and laterally from its base.
cards.att: Base articulates with the cuboid behind and with the fourth metatarsal medially; the head articulates with the proximal phalanx of the little toe. Fibularis brevis inserts on the tuberosity of the base, fibularis tertius on the dorsal surface of the base. Flexor digiti minimi brevis arises from the plantar surface of the base and the sheath of fibularis longus, the third plantar interosseous from the base and medial side of the shaft, and the fourth dorsal interosseous by one head from the medial side of the shaft, its other head from the fourth metatarsal.
cards.act: Forms the lateral border of the foot and transmits weight to the ground at the base and head; anchors the lateral longitudinal arch.
cards.rel: The tuberosity is palpable at the midpoint of the lateral border of the foot and marks the level of the transverse tarsal joint region on the lateral side.
cards.clin: Forced inversion avulses the tuberosity through fibularis brevis and the lateral band of the plantar aponeurosis, the pseudo-Jones fracture; a true Jones fracture at the metaphyseal-diaphyseal junction lies in a watershed zone and is prone to non-union. The apophysis in adolescents lies parallel to the shaft and is mistaken for a fracture.
cards.exam: Q. Which muscle inserts into the tuberosity of the fifth metatarsal? A. Fibularis brevis.

cards.desc: Shortest and stoutest metatarsal, forming the skeleton of the medial border of the forefoot and bearing most of the load at push off.
cards.att: Base articulates with the medial cuneiform and normally has no facet for the second metatarsal; the head articulates with the proximal phalanx of the hallux and is grooved on its plantar surface for two sesamoid bones in the tendon of flexor hallucis brevis. Tibialis anterior inserts on the medial side of the base, fibularis longus on the lateral side of the plantar aspect of the base, and the first dorsal interosseous arises from its lateral shaft.
cards.act: Transmits about twice the load of any other metatarsal head at toe off and forms the anterior pillar of the medial longitudinal arch.
cards.rel: Its head, the ball of the great toe, rests on two sesamoids separated by a crest, with flexor hallucis longus running in the groove between them.
cards.clin: Hallux valgus with metatarsus primus varus produces a bunion over the medial eminence of the head. Sesamoiditis and fracture of the sesamoids cause pain under the first metatarsal head, and the base is the medial anchor of the Lisfranc joint.
cards.exam: Q. Which two tendons insert into the base of the first metatarsal? A. Tibialis anterior on its medial side and fibularis longus on its plantar lateral side.

cards.desc: Largest and most superficial muscle of the gluteal region, giving the buttock its shape.
cards.att: Origin: outer surface of the ilium behind the posterior gluteal line, the posterior surface of the lower sacrum and the side of the coccyx, the sacrotuberous ligament and the aponeurosis of erector spinae. Insertion: upper three quarters into the iliotibial tract of the fascia lata; deeper lower quarter into the gluteal tuberosity of the femur.
cards.sup: Inferior gluteal nerve (L5, S1, S2).
cards.act: Powerful extensor and lateral rotator of the hip, used chiefly in climbing stairs, running and rising from a seated position; through the iliotibial tract it steadies the femur on the tibia in extension.
cards.rel: Covers the short lateral rotators and the structures leaving the greater sciatic foramen, including the sciatic nerve; three bursae lie deep to it, over the greater trochanter, the ischial tuberosity and the gluteal tuberosity.
cards.clin: Intramuscular injections are given in the upper outer quadrant of the buttock to avoid the sciatic nerve, which lies midway between the ischial tuberosity and the greater trochanter. Weakness makes the patient lean the trunk backwards over the affected hip during stance, the gluteus maximus lurch.
cards.exam: Q. Why is the upper outer quadrant of the buttock chosen for intramuscular injection? A. To avoid the sciatic nerve and the gluteal vessels, which lie in the lower and medial quadrants.

cards.desc: Thick fan shaped abductor of the hip lying deep to gluteus maximus on the outer surface of the ilium.
cards.att: Origin: outer surface of the ilium between the posterior and anterior gluteal lines, and the overlying gluteal aponeurosis. Insertion: oblique ridge on the lateral surface of the greater trochanter of the femur.
cards.sup: Superior gluteal nerve (L4, L5, S1).
cards.act: Abducts the thigh; anterior fibres medially rotate it. In walking it prevents the pelvis from dropping on the unsupported side when the opposite foot is off the ground.
cards.rel: Covered posteriorly by gluteus maximus and anteriorly only by fascia; covers gluteus minimus and the superior gluteal vessels and nerve, which run forwards between the two muscles. The trochanteric bursa separates its tendon from the greater trochanter.
cards.clin: Paralysis from a superior gluteal nerve injury, badly placed injection or hip disease gives a positive Trendelenburg sign, the pelvis sagging on the opposite unsupported side when standing on the affected leg. Its tendon degenerates in greater trochanteric pain syndrome.
cards.exam: Q. Standing on the right leg the left side of the pelvis drops. Which muscles and nerve are affected? A. Right gluteus medius and minimus, supplied by the right superior gluteal nerve.

cards.desc: Longest vein in the body, running the whole length of the lower limb in the superficial fascia on its medial side.
cards.att: Begins at the medial end of the dorsal venous arch of the foot, passes anterior to the medial malleolus, ascends the medial side of the leg with the saphenous nerve, passes a hand's breadth behind the medial border of the patella at the knee, ascends the medial thigh, and pierces the cribriform fascia at the saphenous opening about 3.5 cm below and lateral to the pubic tubercle to end in the femoral vein.
cards.sup: Near its termination it receives the superficial epigastric, superficial circumflex iliac and superficial and deep external pudendal veins; along its course it receives the accessory saphenous veins and communicates with the deep veins through perforating veins, notably in the leg.
cards.act: Superficial venous drainage of the medial foot, leg and thigh; contains about 10 to 20 valves that direct flow upwards and inwards.
cards.rel: Accompanied by the saphenous nerve from the knee downwards, and lies with the ilio-inguinal and superficial inguinal lymph nodes near the saphenofemoral junction.
cards.clin: Incompetent valves at the saphenofemoral junction and in perforating veins cause varicose veins, tested by the Trendelenburg test. It is the classic conduit for coronary artery bypass grafting, reversed to allow flow past its valves. Stripping below the knee risks saphenous nerve injury with numbness along the medial leg and foot.
cards.exam: Q. Where does the great saphenous vein pass in relation to the medial malleolus, and which nerve accompanies it there? A. Anterior to the medial malleolus, accompanied by the saphenous nerve.

cards.desc: The larger of the two cusps of the left atrioventricular (mitral) valve, hanging between the mitral orifice and the aortic vestibule.
cards.att: Attached to the anterior third of the mitral annulus and in fibrous continuity with the left and non-coronary cusps of the aortic valve; its free margin and ventricular surface receive chordae tendineae from both the anterolateral and the posteromedial papillary muscles.
cards.act: Closes the mitral orifice in ventricular systole; in diastole it swings back and forms the posterior boundary of the left ventricular outflow tract.
cards.rel: Separates the mitral inflow from the aortic outflow; the aortic valve lies immediately in front of and above it, and the left ventricular outflow tract lies on its ventricular side.
cards.clin: Systolic anterior motion of this leaflet obstructs the outflow tract in hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy. Prolapse of the anterior leaflet directs the regurgitant jet posteriorly on echocardiography. Rheumatic disease thickens and fuses the cusps, giving the fish-mouth mitral stenosis.
cards.exam: Q. Which valve is in fibrous continuity with the anterior mitral leaflet? A. The aortic valve, through its left coronary and non-coronary cusps.

cards.desc: Curved continuation of the ascending aorta in the superior mediastinum, arching upwards, backwards and to the left over the root of the left lung.
cards.att: Begins behind the right half of the manubrium at the level of the sternal angle (T4 to T5 disc) and ends on the left side of the lower border of T4, where it becomes the descending thoracic aorta. Branches in order: brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid artery, left subclavian artery.
cards.sup: Gives the brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid and left subclavian arteries; the ligamentum arteriosum joins its inferior surface to the left pulmonary artery.
cards.act: Conducts the entire cardiac output from the ascending aorta to the head, neck, upper limbs and descending aorta; baroreceptors in its wall, supplied by the vagus, regulate blood pressure.
cards.rel: On its left lie the left phrenic nerve, left vagus and the left superior intercostal vein; the left recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks under it lateral to the ligamentum arteriosum. Medially and below lie the trachea, oesophagus, thoracic duct and left recurrent laryngeal nerve; the left brachiocephalic vein crosses in front.
cards.clin: An aneurysm or a dilated left atrium can stretch the left recurrent laryngeal nerve and cause hoarseness (Ortner cardiovocal syndrome). Postductal coarctation just beyond the left subclavian gives radiofemoral delay, upper limb hypertension and inferior rib notching from enlarged intercostal arteries.
cards.exam: Q. Which nerve hooks around the arch of the aorta and where? A. The left recurrent laryngeal nerve, immediately lateral to the ligamentum arteriosum.

cards.desc: First part of the aorta, about 5 cm long, running upwards, forwards and to the right within the fibrous pericardium.
cards.att: Begins at the aortic orifice of the left ventricle behind the left half of the sternum at the level of the third costal cartilage, and ends at the level of the sternal angle where it becomes the arch. Its origin shows three dilated aortic sinuses (of Valsalva) and ends distally at the sinotubular junction.
cards.sup: Branches: right coronary artery from the right (anterior) aortic sinus and left coronary artery from the left (posterior) aortic sinus; the posterior (non-coronary) sinus gives no branch.
cards.act: Delivers the left ventricular output to the arch, and through the coronary arteries supplies the heart itself during diastole.
cards.rel: Enclosed with the pulmonary trunk in a common sleeve of serous pericardium; the transverse pericardial sinus lies behind it. The right atrium and superior vena cava lie to its right, the pulmonary trunk to its left, and the right pulmonary artery and right main bronchus behind.
cards.clin: Dilatation of the aortic root occurs in Marfan syndrome and cystic medial degeneration. Type A dissection involves the ascending aorta and is a surgical emergency because it can rupture into the pericardium and cause tamponade. Rupture of the ascending aorta bleeds into the pericardial cavity, since this segment is intrapericardial.
cards.exam: Q. Which vessels arise from the ascending aorta? A. Only the right and left coronary arteries, from the corresponding aortic sinuses.

cards.desc: Unpaired vein of the right posterior thoracic wall that links the inferior and superior venae cavae and drains most of the posterior intercostal spaces.
cards.att: Usually formed at about the level of L1 or L2 by the union of the right ascending lumbar vein and the right subcostal vein, sometimes arising from the inferior vena cava; enters the thorax through the aortic hiatus or the right crus, ascends on the right of the vertebral bodies, then arches forwards over the root of the right lung at the level of T4 to open into the superior vena cava.
cards.sup: Tributaries: right posterior intercostal veins of the 4th to 11th spaces, right subcostal vein, hemiazygos and accessory hemiazygos veins, right superior intercostal vein, right bronchial, oesophageal, mediastinal and pericardial veins.
cards.act: Returns blood from the posterior thoracic and upper abdominal walls to the superior vena cava, and provides an alternative route between the caval systems.
cards.rel: Lies to the right of the thoracic duct and the descending thoracic aorta, in front of the vertebral bodies and right posterior intercostal arteries, behind the oesophagus at its arch; the right lung root lies below its arch.
cards.clin: The principal collateral channel in obstruction of the superior or inferior vena cava, when it dilates and is visible on chest radiograph. An azygos lobe of the right lung forms when the vein migrates abnormally through the upper lobe, drawing a fissure with it.
cards.exam: Q. At what level does the azygos vein arch to enter the superior vena cava? A. At the level of T4, arching over the root of the right lung.

cards.desc: Flat middle part of the sternum, formed by fusion of four sternebrae, lying between the manubrium above and the xiphoid process below.
cards.att: Articulates with the manubrium at the manubriosternal joint (sternal angle, a symphysis) and with the xiphoid at the xiphisternal joint. Costal notches take the lower half of the 2nd costal cartilage, the 3rd to 6th cartilages, and the upper part of the 7th. Gives attachment to pectoralis major, to transversus thoracis internally and to the rectus sheath aponeuroses below.
cards.sup: Internal thoracic artery through perforating and sternal branches; contains red marrow throughout life.
cards.act: Protects the mediastinum and forms the anterior anchor of the rib cage, moving forward and upward with the ribs in inspiration.
cards.rel: Behind it lie the anterior mediastinum, the pericardium and the right ventricle with its outflow tract; the internal thoracic vessels descend about 1 cm lateral to its border.
cards.clin: Sternal puncture for marrow aspiration is done in the body at the level of the 2nd or 3rd intercostal space. Median sternotomy splits it for cardiac surgery; the xiphisternal joint lies at the T9 vertebral level.
cards.exam: Q. Which costal cartilages articulate with the body of the sternum? A. The 2nd (lower half) to the 7th (upper part), with the 3rd to 6th articulating with the body alone.

cards.desc: Wide venous channel about 2 to 3 cm long in the posterior part of the coronary sulcus, the main venous drainage of the heart.
cards.att: Lies in the atrioventricular groove between the left atrium and the left ventricle on the diaphragmatic surface, and opens into the right atrium between the opening of the inferior vena cava and the right atrioventricular orifice, guarded by the valve of the coronary sinus (Thebesian valve).
cards.sup: Tributaries: great cardiac vein, middle cardiac vein, small cardiac vein, posterior vein of the left ventricle and the oblique vein of the left atrium (vein of Marshall), which marks its left limit. It is a derivative of the left horn of the sinus venosus.
cards.act: Returns about 60 per cent of the coronary venous blood to the right atrium; the remainder reaches the chambers directly through the anterior cardiac veins and venae cordis minimae.
