cards.rel: Left atrium above, left ventricle below, the circumflex artery running with it in the coronary sulcus; the fibrous pericardium and oblique pericardial sinus lie behind.
cards.clin: Cannulated for retrograde cardioplegia in cardiac surgery and for placing the left ventricular pacing lead in cardiac resynchronisation therapy. It is markedly dilated when a persistent left superior vena cava drains into it, a finding on echocardiography.
cards.exam: Q. Where does the coronary sinus open, and what guards its opening? A. Into the right atrium between the inferior vena caval opening and the right atrioventricular orifice, guarded by the Thebesian valve.

cards.desc: The whole of the aorta beyond the arch, comprising the thoracic part from T4 to T12 and the abdominal part from T12 to its bifurcation at L4.
cards.att: Begins at the lower border of T4 on the left side of the vertebral column as the continuation of the arch, passes through the aortic hiatus of the diaphragm at T12 to become the abdominal aorta, and ends at the level of L4 by dividing into the two common iliac arteries.
cards.sup: Thoracic part: posterior intercostal arteries of the 3rd to 11th spaces, subcostal, bronchial, oesophageal, pericardial, mediastinal and superior phrenic arteries. Abdominal part: inferior phrenic, coeliac trunk, superior mesenteric, middle suprarenal, renal, gonadal, inferior mesenteric, lumbar and median sacral arteries.
cards.act: Supplies the posterior thoracic wall, thoracic viscera, the whole of the abdomen and the lower limbs.
cards.rel: Descends on the left of the vertebral bodies in the thorax and comes to lie in the midline in front of them; the azygos vein and thoracic duct lie to its right, the oesophagus in front, and in the abdomen the inferior vena cava is on its right.
cards.clin: Atherosclerotic aneurysm most often affects the infrarenal abdominal part. Aortic dissection distal to the left subclavian is type B and is usually treated medically or by endovascular stenting.
cards.exam: Q. At what vertebral levels does the descending aorta begin and end? A. It begins at the lower border of T4 and ends at L4 by dividing into the common iliac arteries.

cards.desc: Thoracic segment of the descending aorta, running in the posterior mediastinum from the lower border of T4 to the aortic hiatus of the diaphragm at T12.
cards.att: Begins on the left side of the lower border of T4 as the continuation of the aortic arch, descends on the left of the vertebral bodies gradually coming to the midline, and passes behind the median arcuate ligament through the aortic hiatus at T12 with the thoracic duct and azygos vein.
cards.sup: Branches: posterior intercostal arteries to the 3rd to 11th spaces, subcostal arteries, bronchial, oesophageal, pericardial, mediastinal and superior phrenic arteries.
cards.act: Supplies the posterior thoracic wall, bronchi, oesophagus, pericardium and the posterior part of the diaphragm.
cards.rel: Oesophagus lies to its right above and in front of it below; the azygos vein and thoracic duct lie on its right, the hemiazygos vein behind it, and the left lung and pleura on its left. It is crossed by the left greater splanchnic nerve.
cards.clin: Deceleration injury tears the aorta at the isthmus just distal to the left subclavian origin where the ligamentum arteriosum tethers it, giving a widened mediastinum on chest radiograph. The great anterior radicular artery (of Adamkiewicz), usually from a lower left posterior intercostal artery, supplies the lumbar spinal cord, and its sacrifice in aortic surgery causes paraplegia.
cards.exam: Q. Which structures accompany the aorta through the aortic hiatus at T12? A. The thoracic duct and the azygos vein.

cards.desc: Dome-shaped musculotendinous septum separating the thoracic from the abdominal cavity, the principal muscle of respiration.
cards.att: Origin from three parts: sternal, two slips from the back of the xiphoid process; costal, inner surfaces of the lower six costal cartilages and ribs; lumbar, the right crus from bodies of L1 to L3 and the left crus from L1 to L2, with the medial and lateral arcuate ligaments. All fibres insert into the central tendon.
cards.sup: Motor supply is entirely from the phrenic nerve, C3, C4, C5. Sensory supply to the peripheral part is from the lower intercostal (T7 to T11) and subcostal nerves. Arteries: musculophrenic, pericardiacophrenic, superior and inferior phrenic, lower posterior intercostal.
cards.act: Contraction flattens the domes and increases the vertical diameter of the thorax, the chief movement of quiet inspiration; also raises intra-abdominal pressure in straining, coughing and micturition.
cards.rel: Openings: caval opening in the central tendon at T8 for the inferior vena cava and right phrenic nerve; oesophageal opening in the right crus at T10 for the oesophagus, vagal trunks and oesophageal branches of the left gastric vessels; aortic opening behind the median arcuate ligament at T12 for the aorta, thoracic duct and azygos vein.
cards.clin: Irritation of the central diaphragmatic pleura or peritoneum refers pain to the shoulder tip through C3, C4, C5. Phrenic nerve injury causes a raised hemidiaphragm with paradoxical movement on sniffing. Congenital posterolateral (Bochdalek) and anterior (Morgagni) hernias, and sliding hiatus hernia, occur at its weak points.
cards.exam: Q. Name the structures passing through the diaphragm at T8, T10 and T12. A. T8 inferior vena cava and right phrenic nerve; T10 oesophagus, vagi and left gastric vessels; T12 aorta, thoracic duct and azygos vein.

cards.desc: Typical mid-thoracic vertebra with a heart-shaped body, a small circular vertebral foramen and a long spine directed downwards.
cards.att: Superior costal demifacet for the head of rib 8 and inferior demifacet for the head of rib 9; the transverse process carries a costal facet for the tubercle of rib 8. Articular facets lie in the coronal plane, the superior facing backwards and the inferior forwards.
cards.sup: Segmental branches of the posterior intercostal arteries; sinuvertebral nerves and medial branches of the thoracic dorsal rami supply the periosteum and facet joints.
cards.act: Transmits axial load, protects the spinal cord, and with its coronal facets and attached ribs permits rotation while limiting flexion.
cards.rel: Descending thoracic aorta anterolaterally on the left, azygos vein and thoracic duct on the right, oesophagus in front; the sympathetic trunk crosses the head of the rib laterally.
cards.clin: The caval opening of the diaphragm lies at the T8 level, transmitting the inferior vena cava and the right phrenic nerve. A thoracic disc prolapse at this level compresses the cord itself, causing spastic paraparesis rather than a simple radiculopathy.
cards.exam: Q. Which structures pass through the diaphragm at the T8 level? A. The inferior vena cava and the right phrenic nerve, through the central tendon.

cards.desc: Muscular tube about 25 cm long conveying food from the pharynx to the stomach, running through the neck, posterior mediastinum and a short abdominal segment.
cards.att: Begins at the lower border of the cricoid cartilage at C6 and ends at the cardiac orifice of the stomach at T11, entering the abdomen through the oesophageal hiatus in the right crus of the diaphragm at T10. Upper third is striated muscle, middle third mixed, lower third smooth muscle.
cards.sup: Arteries: inferior thyroid, oesophageal branches of thoracic aorta and bronchial arteries, left gastric and left inferior phrenic. Veins: inferior thyroid and azygos system above, left gastric (portal) below. Nerves: vagi through the oesophageal plexus, with sympathetic fibres. Lymph: deep cervical, posterior mediastinal and left gastric nodes.
cards.act: Propels the bolus by peristalsis; the lower oesophageal sphincter, a physiological sphincter reinforced by the right crus, prevents reflux.
cards.rel: In the thorax it lies behind the trachea and left main bronchus, behind the left atrium, and in front of the vertebral bodies, thoracic duct and descending aorta; it deviates left in the neck and again at the diaphragm. Three constrictions occur at 15 cm (cricopharyngeal), 22 to 27 cm (aortic arch and left main bronchus) and 40 cm (diaphragmatic) from the incisors.
cards.clin: Foreign bodies lodge and carcinoma and strictures arise at the constrictions. Oesophageal varices at the lower end are a portosystemic anastomosis and bleed in portal hypertension. Achalasia shows a bird beak narrowing on barium swallow.
cards.exam: Q. Give the three constrictions of the oesophagus and their distances from the incisor teeth. A. Cricopharyngeal 15 cm, aortic and bronchial 22 to 27 cm, diaphragmatic 40 cm.

cards.desc: Outermost of the three intercostal muscle layers, eleven on each side, filling the posterior and lateral part of each intercostal space.
cards.att: Arises from the lower border of the rib above and inserts into the upper border of the rib below; fibres run downwards, forwards and medially, in the direction of the hands placed in the front trouser pockets. Extends from the tubercle of the rib behind to the costochondral junction in front, where it is replaced by the external intercostal membrane.
cards.sup: Intercostal nerves, the ventral rami of T1 to T11.
cards.act: Elevates the ribs and increases the anteroposterior and transverse diameters of the thorax during inspiration; also supports the intercostal space and resists paradoxical indrawing.
cards.rel: Superficial to the internal intercostal muscle; the neurovascular bundle lies deep to the internal intercostal, not deep to this layer. Covered externally by the serratus anterior, pectoral and back muscles.
cards.clin: An intercostal drain or aspiration needle passes through skin, superficial fascia, external, internal and innermost intercostal muscles and parietal pleura, entering just above the upper border of the lower rib.
cards.exam: Q. What replaces the external intercostal muscle anteriorly? A. The external intercostal membrane, between the costochondral junction and the sternum.

cards.desc: Shortest, broadest and most sharply curved rib, set almost horizontally with superior and inferior surfaces and outer and inner borders.
cards.att: Head has a single facet for the body of T1; short neck; prominent tubercle articulating with the transverse process of T1; the superior surface bears the scalene tubercle for scalenus anterior, with the groove for the subclavian vein in front of it and the groove for the subclavian artery and lower trunk of the brachial plexus behind it. Scalenus medius attaches behind the arterial groove, subclavius near the costal cartilage, and serratus anterior gives its first digitation to it.
cards.sup: Supreme (superior) intercostal artery from the costocervical trunk; the first thoracic nerve contributes chiefly to the brachial plexus rather than running as a typical intercostal nerve.
cards.act: Its elevation raises the whole rib cage in inspiration; it forms the bony boundary of the thoracic inlet and anchors the suprapleural membrane.
cards.rel: The cervical pleura and apex of the lung rise above its inner border, roofed by the suprapleural membrane of Sibson attached to it; the subclavian vessels and lower trunk of the brachial plexus cross it; the clavicle lies above.
cards.clin: A cervical rib or fibrous band compressing the lower trunk and subclavian artery over the 1st rib produces thoracic outlet syndrome with T1 wasting of the small hand muscles. The 1st rib is deeply protected, so its fracture indicates severe trauma and raises suspicion of great vessel injury.
cards.exam: Q. What separates the grooves for the subclavian artery and vein on the first rib? A. The scalene tubercle, the insertion of scalenus anterior.

cards.desc: Typical upper thoracic vertebra whose lower border, with the T4/T5 disc, lies in the plane of the sternal angle.
cards.att: Superior demifacet for the head of rib 4 and inferior demifacet for the head of rib 5; the transverse process carries a facet for the tubercle of rib 4; the long spine slopes downwards over the vertebra below.
cards.sup: Segmental posterior intercostal branches; dorsal rami to the facets and periosteum.
cards.act: Load transmission, cord protection and rib articulation permitting rotation.
cards.rel: The arch of the aorta arches backwards and to the left across its body; the trachea bifurcates and the azygos vein arches forward over the right main bronchus at this level; the oesophagus and thoracic duct lie in front.
cards.clin: The transverse thoracic plane through the sternal angle and the T4/T5 disc separates superior from inferior mediastinum and marks the tracheal bifurcation, the beginning and end of the aortic arch and the level of the 2nd costal cartilage. The T4 dermatome lies at the nipple line, used to check the height of a spinal block.
cards.exam: Q. Name three structures found at the level of the sternal angle. A. Bifurcation of the trachea, the beginning and end of the arch of the aorta, and the articulation of the 2nd costal cartilage, all at the T4/T5 disc.

cards.desc: Middle of the three intercostal layers, eleven on each side, with fibres running at right angles to those of the external intercostal.
cards.att: Arises from the floor of the costal groove of the rib above and from the costal cartilage, and inserts into the upper border of the rib below; fibres run downwards and backwards. Extends from the sternum in front to the angles of the ribs behind, where it is replaced by the internal intercostal membrane.
cards.sup: Intercostal nerves, the ventral rami of T1 to T11.
cards.act: The interosseous part depresses the ribs in forced expiration; the interchondral part, between the costal cartilages, elevates the ribs in inspiration.
cards.rel: Deep to the external intercostal, superficial to the intercostal neurovascular bundle and the innermost intercostal muscle.
cards.clin: Posteriorly, where only the internal intercostal membrane is present, a paravertebral injection spreads readily to adjacent levels. Intercostal muscle tears cause sharp pleuritic-type pain worse on coughing.
cards.exam: Q. Which part of the internal intercostal muscle assists inspiration? A. The interchondral part, between the costal cartilages.

cards.desc: Long branch of the first part of the subclavian artery descending just lateral to the sternum behind the upper six costal cartilages.
cards.att: Arises from the inferior surface of the first part of the subclavian artery opposite the thyrocervical trunk, enters the thorax behind the clavicle and first costal cartilage, descends about 1 to 1.25 cm lateral to the sternal border, and divides at the level of the sixth intercostal space into the superior epigastric and musculophrenic arteries.
cards.sup: Branches: pericardiacophrenic, mediastinal, thymic, sternal, anterior intercostal arteries to the upper six spaces, perforating branches with medial mammary branches, and the terminal superior epigastric and musculophrenic arteries.
cards.act: Supplies the anterior chest wall, sternum, thymus, pericardium, medial part of the breast and, through the superior epigastric artery, the upper anterior abdominal wall.
cards.rel: Above the second costal cartilage it lies on the pleura, below that it is separated from the pleura by transversus thoracis; the phrenic nerve crosses it in front from lateral to medial at the thoracic inlet. Parasternal (internal thoracic) lymph nodes lie alongside it.
cards.clin: The left internal thoracic artery is the graft of choice to the left anterior descending coronary artery, with the best long-term patency. Medial quadrant breast cancer spreads to the parasternal nodes along it. In coarctation of the aorta its enlarged anterior intercostal branches produce inferior rib notching.
cards.exam: Q. Into which two arteries does the internal thoracic artery divide, and where? A. Superior epigastric and musculophrenic arteries, in the sixth intercostal space.

cards.desc: The left principal bronchus, conducting air from the tracheal bifurcation to the left lung; narrower, longer and more horizontal than its right counterpart.
cards.att: Begins at the carina at the level of the sternal angle (T4 to T5) and runs about 5 cm downwards and laterally at roughly 45 degrees to the midline, entering the hilum of the left lung where it divides into superior and inferior lobar bronchi.
cards.sup: Bronchial arteries from the thoracic aorta, usually two on the left; venous drainage to the accessory hemiazygos and azygos veins; nerves from the pulmonary plexuses, vagal and sympathetic.
cards.act: Conducts air; its cartilaginous rings hold the lumen open and the ciliated respiratory epithelium clears mucus towards the trachea.
cards.rel: Passes below the arch of the aorta and in front of the oesophagus and descending thoracic aorta. At the hilum the left pulmonary artery lies above it and the pulmonary veins in front and below.
cards.clin: Widening of the carinal angle on chest radiograph or bronchoscopy suggests subcarinal nodal disease or gross left atrial enlargement, which can also compress the left main bronchus. A left sided double lumen endobronchial tube is standard for one lung ventilation.
cards.exam: Q. Why do inhaled foreign bodies rarely enter the left main bronchus? A. It is narrower, longer and more oblique than the right main bronchus.

cards.desc: Smaller terminal branch of the internal carotid artery, supplying the medial surface of the frontal and parietal lobes.
cards.att: Arises at the bifurcation of the internal carotid lateral to the optic chiasm, runs medially above the optic nerve (A1), joins its fellow by the anterior communicating artery, then turns up in the longitudinal fissure and arches round the genu of the corpus callosum as the pericallosal artery, ending near the parieto-occipital sulcus.
cards.sup: Medial striate artery (recurrent artery of Heubner), medial frontobasal (orbitofrontal), frontopolar, callosomarginal with its paracentral branch, and pericallosal arteries.
cards.act: Supplies the medial surface of the cerebral hemisphere from the frontal pole to the parieto-occipital sulcus, a strip over the superolateral margin including the leg area of the paracentral lobule, the corpus callosum, and, through Heubner artery, the head of the caudate and anterior limb of the internal capsule.
cards.rel: Lies above the optic nerve and chiasm at its origin, in the longitudinal fissure between the hemispheres, on the corpus callosum; forms the anterior part of the circle of Willis with the anterior communicating artery.
cards.clin: Occlusion causes contralateral weakness and sensory loss maximal in the lower limb, urinary incontinence and abulia, sparing the face and hand. The anterior communicating artery is a common site of berry aneurysm, whose rupture or expansion can compress the optic chiasm.
cards.exam: Q. Which part of the body is chiefly affected in anterior cerebral artery occlusion, and why? A. The contralateral lower limb, because the leg area lies in the paracentral lobule on the medial surface supplied by this artery.

cards.desc: C-shaped mass of grey matter of the corpus striatum arching over the thalamus and following the concavity of the lateral ventricle, with a head, body and tail.
cards.att: Head bulges into the floor and lateral wall of the anterior horn of the lateral ventricle; the body lies in the floor of the ventricular body; the tail curves into the roof of the inferior horn and ends in the amygdaloid body. Joined to the putamen by grey bridges crossing the anterior limb of the internal capsule.
cards.sup: Head supplied by the medial striate artery of Heubner from the anterior cerebral artery; body and tail by lateral striate (lenticulostriate) branches of the middle cerebral artery and the anterior choroidal artery.
cards.act: With the putamen forms the striatum, the input station of the basal ganglia, concerned with the initiation and control of movement and with cognitive and associative motor learning.
cards.rel: Separated from the lentiform nucleus by the internal capsule; the thalamus lies medial to its body with the stria terminalis and thalamostriate vein in the intervening groove; the lateral ventricle lies on its ventricular surface.
cards.clin: Selective atrophy of the caudate head in Huntington's disease produces the boxcar appearance of dilated frontal horns on CT and MRI. Infarction of the head from occlusion of Heubner's artery may cause abulia and contralateral facio-brachial weakness.
cards.exam: Q. What separates the caudate nucleus from the lentiform nucleus? A. The internal capsule, crossed by grey bridges of striatum.

cards.desc: Narrow ependyma-lined canal running the whole length of the spinal cord within the grey commissure, the persistent lumen of the embryonic neural tube.
cards.att: Continuous above with the cavity of the fourth ventricle at the level of the obex; expands below in the conus medullaris as the terminal ventricle.
cards.act: Contains cerebrospinal fluid; largely obliterated in the adult and of no significant conducting function.
cards.rel: Lies in the grey commissure between the anterior and posterior grey commissures, with the anterior white commissure in front of it and the posterior median septum behind.
cards.clin: Pathological cavitation around the canal, syringomyelia, interrupts the decussating spinothalamic fibres in the anterior white commissure and produces a suspended, cape-like dissociated sensory loss of pain and temperature with preserved touch and proprioception.
cards.exam: Q. Why is sensory loss dissociated in syringomyelia? A. The cavity interrupts decussating pain and temperature fibres in the anterior white commissure while the dorsal columns are spared.

cards.desc: Largest part of the hindbrain, lying in the posterior cranial fossa behind the pons and medulla and below the tentorium cerebelli, consisting of two hemispheres joined by the median vermis.
cards.att: Attached to the brainstem by three paired peduncles: superior to the midbrain, middle to the pons, inferior to the medulla. Divided by the primary fissure into anterior and posterior lobes and by the posterolateral fissure into the flocculonodular lobe.
cards.sup: Superior cerebellar artery from the basilar, anterior inferior cerebellar artery from the basilar, and posterior inferior cerebellar artery from the vertebral artery.
cards.act: Coordination of movement, regulation of muscle tone and posture, maintenance of equilibrium, and motor learning. Vestibulocerebellum controls balance and eye movements, spinocerebellum posture and gait, cerebrocerebellum planning and timing of skilled movement.
cards.rel: Fourth ventricle lies in front of it between it and the pons and medulla; tentorium cerebelli separates it from the occipital lobes above; the cerebellar tonsils lie close to the foramen magnum.
cards.clin: Cerebellar lesions produce signs on the same side as the lesion: intention tremor, dysdiadochokinesia, dysmetria, nystagmus, scanning speech and hypotonia. Midline vermian lesions give truncal ataxia, and medulloblastoma of the vermis is a common posterior fossa tumour of childhood; raised pressure may force the tonsils through the foramen magnum.
cards.exam: Q. Why are cerebellar signs ipsilateral to the lesion? A. Because cerebellar output pathways cross twice, in the superior cerebellar peduncle decussation and again in the corticospinal decussation.

cards.desc: Narrow ependyma-lined channel about 15 to 18 mm long traversing the midbrain and joining the third to the fourth ventricle.
cards.att: Connects the third ventricle above with the fourth ventricle below; surrounded by the periaqueductal (central) grey matter.
cards.act: Conducts cerebrospinal fluid from the third to the fourth ventricle. It contains no choroid plexus.
cards.rel: Separates the tectum behind from the tegmentum in front; the oculomotor nucleus and trochlear nucleus lie in the periaqueductal grey ventral to it at superior and inferior collicular levels respectively.
cards.clin: Being the narrowest part of the ventricular system, the aqueduct is the commonest site of obstruction; congenital stenosis or a pineal or tectal tumour causes non-communicating (obstructive) hydrocephalus with dilated lateral and third ventricles and a normal fourth ventricle.
cards.exam: Q. Which ventricular dilatation pattern indicates aqueduct stenosis? A. Dilated lateral and third ventricles with a normal-sized fourth ventricle.

cards.desc: The largest commissure of the brain, a thick arched plate of white matter in the floor of the longitudinal fissure connecting the neocortex of the two hemispheres.
cards.att: From front to back: rostrum, genu, trunk (body) and splenium. Fibres of the genu sweep forward as the forceps minor into the frontal lobes, those of the splenium sweep back as the forceps major into the occipital lobes, and fibres passing laterally over the lateral ventricle form the tapetum.
cards.sup: Pericallosal artery from the anterior cerebral artery along most of its length; the splenium is also supplied by the posterior pericallosal branch of the posterior cerebral artery.
cards.act: Interhemispheric transfer of sensory, motor and cognitive information between corresponding cortical areas.
cards.rel: Forms the roof of the lateral ventricles and of the third ventricle region; the cingulate gyrus lies above it across the callosal sulcus, the fornix and septum pellucidum below the trunk, and the anterior cerebral arteries run on its upper surface.
cards.clin: Section of the corpus callosum for intractable epilepsy produces disconnection syndromes including alien hand. Infarction of the splenium with the left occipital cortex produces alexia without agraphia: the patient can write but cannot read what has been written.
cards.exam: Q. Which part of the corpus callosum is damaged in alexia without agraphia? A. The splenium, together with the left occipital cortex.

cards.desc: Arched bundle of white matter forming the principal efferent pathway of the hippocampal formation, running from the temporal lobe beneath the corpus callosum to the hypothalamus.
cards.att: Begins as the alveus on the ventricular surface of the hippocampus, gathers as the fimbria, becomes the crus, the two crura join beneath the corpus callosum to form the body, which divides in front into the two columns; postcommissural fibres end mainly in the mammillary body and precommissural fibres in the septal region.
cards.act: Carries hippocampal output to the mammillary body, septal nuclei and anterior thalamus; a key limb of the Papez circuit and of memory consolidation.
cards.rel: Body forms the roof of the third ventricle with the tela choroidea; the column forms the anterior boundary of the interventricular foramen, with the anterior tubercle of the thalamus behind. The crura lie beneath the splenium, joined by the commissure of the fornix.
cards.clin: Bilateral damage to the fornix, for example during removal of a third ventricular colloid cyst or from a midline tumour, causes anterograde amnesia. A colloid cyst wedged between the columns at the interventricular foramen causes acute obstructive hydrocephalus with positional headache and drop attacks.
cards.exam: Q. What forms the anterior boundary of the interventricular foramen? A. The column of the fornix.

cards.desc: Tent-shaped cavity of the hindbrain lying between the pons and upper medulla in front and the cerebellum behind, diamond-shaped in its floor.
cards.att: Continuous above with the cerebral aqueduct and below with the central canal of the medulla; communicates with the subarachnoid space through the median aperture of Magendie and the paired lateral apertures of Luschka.
cards.act: Contains cerebrospinal fluid and, through its apertures, is the only route by which cerebrospinal fluid leaves the ventricular system for the subarachnoid space.
cards.rel: Floor, the rhomboid fossa, is formed by the posterior surface of the pons and open part of the medulla and overlies the cranial nerve nuclei, with the facial colliculus, median sulcus, sulcus limitans, vestibular area and hypoglossal and vagal trigones. Roof is formed above by the superior cerebellar peduncles and superior medullary velum, below by the inferior medullary velum and tela choroidea.
cards.clin: Obstruction of the outlet foramina, as in Dandy-Walker malformation, causes hydrocephalus with a grossly dilated fourth ventricle. A lesion at the facial colliculus damages the abducent nucleus and the looping facial fibres, giving ipsilateral lateral rectus palsy with lower motor neuron facial palsy.
cards.exam: Q. Name the apertures of the fourth ventricle. A. The median aperture of Magendie and the two lateral apertures of Luschka.

cards.desc: Pale, heavily myelinated medial part of the lentiform nucleus, wedge-shaped in horizontal section, lying medial to the putamen and lateral to the internal capsule.
cards.att: Divided by the medial medullary lamina into external and internal segments and separated from the putamen by the lateral medullary lamina. Receives from the striatum and subthalamic nucleus; the internal segment projects to the thalamus through the ansa lenticularis and lenticular fasciculus, which join as the thalamic fasciculus.
cards.sup: Lenticulostriate branches of the middle cerebral artery and the anterior choroidal artery.
cards.act: Principal output nucleus of the basal ganglia, regulating the thalamocortical drive to the motor cortex and thereby the scaling and smoothness of voluntary movement.
cards.rel: Lateral to the genu and posterior limb of the internal capsule and to the caudate nucleus and thalamus beyond it; the putamen lies lateral, and the optic tract and substantia innominata lie below.
cards.clin: The internal segment is the classic target for pallidotomy and for deep brain stimulation in Parkinson's disease and dystonia. Bilateral pallidal necrosis is characteristic of carbon monoxide poisoning.
cards.exam: Q. Which structure separates the globus pallidus from the putamen? A. The lateral medullary lamina.

cards.desc: Curved elevation of three-layered archicortex in the floor of the inferior horn of the lateral ventricle, formed by the medial temporal lobe rolling into the ventricle along the hippocampal fissure.
cards.att: Its expanded anterior end is the pes hippocampi; the ventricular surface is covered by the white alveus, whose fibres gather medially as the fimbria and continue as the crus of the fornix. Principal input is from the entorhinal cortex of the parahippocampal gyrus by the perforant path; output is through the fornix to the mammillary body and septal nuclei.
cards.sup: Branches of the anterior choroidal artery and hippocampal branches of the posterior cerebral artery.
cards.act: Formation and consolidation of new declarative (episodic) memory and spatial memory.
cards.rel: Lies in the floor of the inferior horn of the lateral ventricle with the choroid plexus above it along the choroid fissure; the dentate gyrus lies medial and the parahippocampal gyrus and subiculum below and medial; the tail of the caudate nucleus lies in the ventricular roof.
cards.clin: Mesial temporal sclerosis, with neuronal loss maximal in the CA1 (Sommer) sector, is the commonest pathology in drug-resistant temporal lobe epilepsy and is treated by anterior temporal lobectomy with amygdalohippocampectomy. Bilateral hippocampal damage causes a dense anterograde amnesia, and the hippocampus is the earliest cortical region to atrophy in Alzheimer's disease.
cards.exam: Q. What deficit follows bilateral hippocampal destruction? A. Anterograde amnesia, an inability to form new declarative memories, with old memories retained.

cards.desc: Small region of the diencephalon forming the floor and the lower part of the lateral wall of the third ventricle, below the hypothalamic sulcus.
cards.att: Extends from the lamina terminalis and optic chiasm in front to the mammillary bodies and posterior perforated substance behind; includes the optic chiasm, tuber cinereum with median eminence, infundibulum and mammillary bodies. Receives the fornix and stria terminalis; the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei send the hypothalamohypophysial tract to the neurohypophysis, and the median eminence gives the hypophysial portal vessels to the adenohypophysis.
cards.sup: Branches of the circle of Willis, chiefly the anterior and posterior communicating and posterior cerebral arteries.
cards.act: Chief integrator of the autonomic nervous system and controller of the endocrine system: regulates temperature, appetite and thirst, water balance, sleep and circadian rhythm, sexual behaviour and emotional expression.
cards.rel: Thalamus lies above across the hypothalamic sulcus; the third ventricle is medial; the internal capsule and subthalamus lie laterally; the pituitary gland hangs below from the infundibulum, with the optic chiasm in front of the stalk.
cards.clin: Damage to the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei or the pituitary stalk causes cranial diabetes insipidus with polyuria and dilute urine. Craniopharyngioma and suprasellar germinoma in this region cause growth failure, visual field loss and endocrine disturbance.
cards.exam: Q. Which hypothalamic nuclei produce the hormones released from the posterior pituitary? A. The supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei, producing vasopressin and oxytocin.

cards.desc: Lower and smaller of the two pairs of rounded eminences of the midbrain tectum, at the level of the caudal midbrain.
cards.att: Receives the lateral lemniscus as its principal input and projects through the brachium of the inferior colliculus to the medial geniculate body; also connected to the superior colliculus and to the contralateral inferior colliculus.
cards.sup: Branches of the superior cerebellar artery and the posterior cerebral artery.
cards.act: Obligatory relay of the ascending auditory pathway; concerned with sound localisation and with reflex turning of the head and eyes towards sound.
cards.rel: Lies below the superior colliculus on the dorsal surface of the midbrain; the trochlear nerve emerges from the dorsal surface immediately below it, and the superior medullary velum and superior cerebellar peduncles lie below and behind.
cards.clin: The dorsal surface just below the inferior colliculus is where the trochlear nerve, the only cranial nerve to leave the brainstem dorsally, emerges and decussates; this makes it vulnerable in tectal lesions and in head injury.
cards.exam: Q. Which cranial nerve emerges just below the inferior colliculus? A. The trochlear nerve, cranial nerve IV.

cards.desc: Lowest of the three gyri on the lateral surface of the frontal lobe, lying between the inferior frontal sulcus above and the lateral sulcus below.
cards.att: Divided by the anterior horizontal and anterior ascending rami of the lateral sulcus into pars orbitalis in front, pars triangularis between, and pars opercularis behind. Connected to the posterior superior temporal region by the arcuate fasciculus.
cards.sup: Branches of the superior division of the middle cerebral artery.
cards.act: Pars opercularis and pars triangularis of the dominant hemisphere form Broca's motor speech area (areas 44 and 45), which programmes the motor production of speech.
cards.rel: Lies above the lateral sulcus and the insula, in front of the precentral gyrus; the middle frontal gyrus lies above across the inferior frontal sulcus.
cards.clin: A lesion of Broca's area, usually an infarct in the superior division of the left middle cerebral artery, causes an expressive (non-fluent) aphasia: speech is sparse and effortful with agrammatism, comprehension is relatively preserved, and repetition is impaired, often with a right hemiparesis worse in the face and arm.
cards.exam: Q. Which parts of the inferior frontal gyrus form Broca's area? A. Pars opercularis and pars triangularis of the dominant hemisphere, Brodmann areas 44 and 45.

cards.desc: Compact, V-shaped sheet of projection fibres, seen in horizontal section with its concavity outwards, lying between the caudate nucleus and thalamus medially and the lentiform nucleus laterally.
cards.att: Divided into an anterior limb between the caudate head and lentiform nucleus, a genu, a posterior limb between the thalamus and lentiform nucleus, and retrolentiform and sublentiform parts. Carries corticonuclear fibres in the genu, corticospinal fibres in the anterior part of the posterior limb, thalamocortical and corticopontine fibres, the optic radiation in the retrolentiform part and the acoustic radiation in the sublentiform part. Continuous above with the corona radiata and below with the crus cerebri.
cards.sup: Lenticulostriate branches of the middle cerebral artery to most of it, the medial striate artery of Heubner to the anterior limb, and the anterior choroidal artery to the lower part of the posterior limb.
cards.act: Conveys almost all afferent and efferent fibres between the cerebral cortex and the brainstem and spinal cord.
cards.rel: Caudate head and thalamus lie medial, lentiform nucleus lateral; the tail of the caudate and the optic radiation lie behind and below.
cards.clin: Because the fibres are packed together, a small lacunar infarct or a hypertensive haemorrhage from a lenticulostriate artery in the posterior limb causes a dense contralateral hemiplegia and hemianaesthesia with no cortical signs such as aphasia or neglect. Extension into the retrolentiform part adds a contralateral homonymous hemianopia.
cards.exam: Q. Where in the internal capsule do corticospinal fibres lie? A. In the anterior part of the posterior limb, with corticonuclear fibres in the genu.

cards.desc: Deep midline depression on the ventral surface of the midbrain between the two diverging crura cerebri.
cards.att: Bounded laterally by the crura cerebri, in front by the mammillary bodies and optic tracts, and behind by the upper border of the pons; its floor is the posterior perforated substance, pierced by central branches of the posterior cerebral and posterior communicating arteries.
cards.act: Contains no neural tissue of its own; it transmits the oculomotor nerves and the central perforating arteries and holds the interpeduncular cistern of cerebrospinal fluid.
cards.rel: The oculomotor nerve emerges from its side wall; the posterior cerebral and superior cerebellar arteries and the basilar bifurcation lie within the interpeduncular cistern here, with the posterior communicating artery running forwards along its lateral edge.
cards.clin: An uncal herniation pushes the medial temporal lobe into this space and compresses the oculomotor nerve against the free edge of the tentorium, giving a fixed dilated pupil and a down-and-out eye on the side of the lesion, followed by contralateral hemiparesis. A posterior communicating artery aneurysm in the same region causes an isolated painful third nerve palsy with a dilated pupil.
cards.exam: Q. Which nerve emerges in the interpeduncular fossa? A. The oculomotor nerve, cranial nerve III.

cards.desc: Short, curved, slit-like channel on each side connecting the lateral ventricle with the third ventricle.
cards.att: Bounded in front by the column of the fornix and behind by the anterior tubercle of the thalamus; the choroid plexus of the lateral ventricle passes through it to become continuous with that of the third ventricle.
cards.act: Conducts cerebrospinal fluid from the lateral ventricle to the third ventricle.
cards.rel: Lies at the junction of the roof and the anterior wall of the third ventricle; the septal and thalamostriate veins unite near it to form the internal cerebral vein, and it is the anatomical origin of the venous angle seen on angiography.
cards.clin: A colloid cyst of the third ventricle lodged at the foramina causes intermittent obstruction with severe positional headache, drop attacks and sudden death, and produces symmetrical dilatation of both lateral ventricles with a normal third ventricle. It is also the target of endoscopic access to the third ventricle.
cards.exam: Q. What are the boundaries of the interventricular foramen? A. The column of the fornix in front and the anterior tubercle of the thalamus behind.

cards.desc: Small oval swelling on the posteroinferior aspect of the thalamus, below the pulvinar, forming the thalamic relay of the visual pathway.
cards.att: Receives the lateral (larger) root of the optic tract and gives rise to the optic radiation (geniculocalcarine tract), which runs through the retrolentiform part of the internal capsule to the visual cortex on the banks of the calcarine sulcus. It has six laminae: layers 1, 4 and 6 receive crossed (contralateral nasal) fibres and layers 2, 3 and 5 uncrossed (ipsilateral temporal) fibres; layers 1 and 2 are magnocellular and layers 3 to 6 parvocellular.
cards.sup: Anterior choroidal artery and the lateral posterior choroidal branch of the posterior cerebral artery.
cards.act: Relays and processes visual information from the retina to the primary visual cortex, keeping the two eyes' inputs in separate layers.
cards.rel: Lies below the pulvinar, lateral to the medial geniculate body, above and lateral to the crus cerebri; the optic tract winds round the crus to reach it.
cards.clin: A lesion of the lateral geniculate body causes a contralateral homonymous hemianopia, often incongruous. Its dual arterial supply produces characteristic sector field defects when one of the two feeding arteries is occluded.
cards.exam: Q. Which lateral geniculate laminae receive crossed retinal fibres? A. Laminae 1, 4 and 6.

cards.desc: The aqueous-filled space of the eyeball bounded in front by the cornea and behind by the iris and the pupillary part of the lens.
cards.att: Bounded anteriorly by the corneal endothelium, posteriorly by the anterior surface of the iris and the central lens, and peripherally by the iridocorneal angle, where the trabecular meshwork and the scleral venous sinus (canal of Schlemm) lie. It communicates with the posterior chamber through the pupil.
cards.act: Holds aqueous humour, which nourishes the avascular cornea and lens and maintains intra-ocular pressure. Aqueous is secreted by the ciliary processes into the posterior chamber, flows through the pupil, and drains through the trabecular meshwork into the scleral venous sinus and thence to the anterior ciliary veins.
cards.rel: Lies in front of the iris and behind the cornea; the angle recess is bounded by the root of the iris and the anterior surface of the ciliary body.
cards.clin: Obstruction at the iridocorneal angle causes acute angle-closure glaucoma with a painful red eye, a fixed mid-dilated pupil and a hazy cornea, treated by laser iridotomy. Blood in the chamber is a hyphaema and pus is a hypopyon.
cards.exam: Q. What is the route of aqueous humour drainage? A. Ciliary processes to posterior chamber, through the pupil to the anterior chamber, then trabecular meshwork to the scleral venous sinus.

cards.desc: Terminal continuation of the nasociliary nerve that leaves the orbit medially and reaches the nasal cavity and the skin of the tip of the nose.
cards.att: Arises from the nasociliary nerve in the medial orbit, leaves through the anterior ethmoidal foramen, runs across the cribriform plate area beneath the dura, descends into the nasal cavity through the nasal slit beside the crista galli, and emerges between the nasal bone and the lateral nasal cartilage as the external nasal nerve.
cards.act: Sensory to the mucosa of the anterosuperior nasal septum and lateral wall, the anterior ethmoidal air cells, and the skin of the dorsum and tip of the nose.
cards.rel: Runs with the anterior ethmoidal artery along the roof of the ethmoid at the frontoethmoidal suture, between the medial rectus and superior oblique in the orbit.
cards.clin: Vesicles on the tip of the nose in herpes zoster ophthalmicus, Hutchinson's sign, follow this nerve's external nasal branch and warn of ocular involvement, because both come from the nasociliary. It is the afferent limb of the sneeze reflex, and its accompanying artery is ligated for bleeding from the anterosuperior part of the nasal septum.
cards.exam: Q. What is the anatomical basis of Hutchinson's sign? A. The external nasal branch of the anterior ethmoidal nerve and the ciliary nerves both arise from the nasociliary nerve.

cards.desc: Paired pyramidal hyaline cartilage sitting on the upper border of the lamina of the cricoid at the back of the larynx.
cards.att: Has an apex bearing the corniculate cartilage, a base articulating with the cricoid at the synovial cricoarytenoid joint, an anteriorly directed vocal process giving attachment to the vocal ligament and conus elasticus, and a laterally directed muscular process receiving posterior cricoarytenoid behind and lateral cricoarytenoid in front. Thyroarytenoid and vocalis attach to its anterolateral surface, the transverse and oblique arytenoids to its posterior surface.
cards.sup: Laryngeal branches of the superior and inferior thyroid arteries; motor supply of all attached muscles is the recurrent laryngeal nerve.
cards.act: Rotation and gliding at the cricoarytenoid joint swing the vocal process laterally or medially, thereby abducting or adducting the vocal fold and altering the length and tension of the vocal ligament.
cards.rel: Piriform fossa lies lateral to it, the laryngeal inlet and aryepiglottic fold anterolateral, the cricoid below and the corniculate cartilage above.
cards.clin: Arytenoid subluxation or dislocation is a recognised complication of difficult intubation and presents with hoarseness and a fixed cord. Recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy leaves the cord in the paramedian position because the arytenoid cannot be abducted.
cards.exam: Q. Which muscle attaches to the muscular process of the arytenoid to abduct the vocal cord? A. Posterior cricoarytenoid, the only abductor of the vocal cord.

cards.desc: Ring-shaped first cervical vertebra with no body and no spine, carrying the skull.
cards.att: Consists of anterior and posterior arches and two lateral masses with transverse processes containing foramina transversaria. The anterior arch bears the anterior tubercle in front and a facet for the dens behind; the posterior arch bears the posterior tubercle and a groove for the vertebral artery and the first cervical nerve. Concave superior facets articulate with the occipital condyles, flattish inferior facets with the axis. The transverse ligament attaches to tubercles on the medial surfaces of the lateral masses.
cards.sup: Vertebral artery grooves the posterior arch; segmental supply from the vertebral and ascending cervical arteries.
cards.act: Transmits the weight of the skull to the axis; the atlanto-occipital joints allow flexion and extension, the nodding movement of yes.
cards.rel: Transverse process is palpable between the mastoid process and the angle of the mandible. The vertebral artery, internal carotid artery, internal jugular vein and the last four cranial nerves lie close to the transverse process.
cards.clin: Axial loading, as in diving into shallow water, splits the ring as a Jefferson burst fracture, usually without cord injury because the fragments spread outwards. Rupture of the transverse ligament allows atlanto-axial subluxation and cord compression.
cards.exam: Q. Why does the atlas have no body? A. Its body has fused with the axis to form the dens, which is retained against the anterior arch by the transverse ligament of the atlas.

cards.desc: Second cervical vertebra, identified by the dens projecting upwards from its body.
cards.att: The dens has an anterior facet for the anterior arch of the atlas, a posterior groove for the transverse ligament, and gives attachment to the apical ligament at its tip and the alar ligaments from its sides to the occipital condyles. Large superior articular facets lie on the body and pedicles for the atlas, a strong bifid spine gives attachment to semispinalis cervicis and the inferior oblique, and the foramina transversaria transmit the vertebral arteries.
cards.sup: Segmental branches of the vertebral and ascending pharyngeal arteries.
cards.act: Forms the pivot for the median and lateral atlanto-axial joints, at which the atlas and skull rotate, the movement of shaking the head for no; about half of all cervical rotation occurs here.
cards.rel: The dens lies behind the anterior arch of the atlas and in front of the transverse ligament and the spinal cord. The vertebral artery turns laterally over the axis before ascending to the atlas.
cards.clin: Fracture of the dens, especially type II at its base, unites poorly and threatens the cord. Hyperextension injury fractures the pars interarticularis bilaterally, the hangman fracture or traumatic spondylolisthesis of C2. The dens erodes in rheumatoid arthritis, so intubation risks atlanto-axial subluxation.
cards.exam: Q. What keeps the dens in place and what happens if it fails? A. The transverse ligament of the atlas; rupture or dens fracture allows atlanto-axial dislocation and compression of the spinal cord.

cards.desc: Single midline artery on the ventral surface of the pons, formed by the union of the two vertebral arteries, supplying the pons, cerebellum and inner ear.
cards.att: Formed at the lower border of the pons (pontomedullary junction) by the union of the two vertebral arteries, ascends in the basilar sulcus of the pons within the pontine cistern, and divides at the upper border of the pons into the two posterior cerebral arteries.
cards.sup: Branches: anterior inferior cerebellar artery, labyrinthine (internal auditory) artery, pontine branches, superior cerebellar artery, and the terminal posterior cerebral arteries.
cards.act: Supplies the pons, midbrain, cerebellum, internal ear and, through the posterior cerebral arteries, the occipital and inferomedial temporal lobes.
cards.rel: Lies on the clivus behind the dorsum sellae, with the abducent nerve emerging at the pontomedullary junction beside it and the oculomotor nerve passing between the superior cerebellar and posterior cerebral arteries at its termination.
cards.clin: Basilar occlusion causes bilateral pontine infarction and the locked-in syndrome: quadriplegia and anarthria with preserved consciousness and vertical eye movement. Occlusion of the labyrinthine artery causes sudden ipsilateral deafness and vertigo.
cards.exam: Q. Which nerve passes between the superior cerebellar and posterior cerebral arteries? A. The oculomotor nerve, hence its compression by a posterior communicating aneurysm or uncal herniation.

cards.desc: Small parasympathetic ganglion, about 2 mm across, lying in the posterior orbit between the optic nerve and lateral rectus, about 1 cm in front of the optic canal.
cards.att: Parasympathetic (motor) root from the nerve to inferior oblique, from the inferior branch of the oculomotor nerve, carrying preganglionic fibres from the Edinger-Westphal nucleus that synapse here. Sensory root from the nasociliary nerve and sympathetic root from the internal carotid plexus both pass through without synapsing. Its branches are the short ciliary nerves.
cards.act: Relay station for parasympathetic supply to sphincter pupillae and ciliary muscle, mediating the light reflex and accommodation.
cards.rel: Lies lateral to the optic nerve and medial to lateral rectus, with the ophthalmic artery above and the short ciliary nerves passing forwards from it around the optic nerve.
cards.clin: Damage or a viral ganglionitis produces a tonic (Adie) pupil: a dilated pupil with light-near dissociation, sector palsy of the iris and denervation supersensitivity to dilute pilocarpine.
cards.exam: Q. Which fibres actually synapse in the ciliary ganglion? A. Only the preganglionic parasympathetic fibres from the oculomotor nerve; sensory and sympathetic fibres pass through.

cards.desc: Main arterial trunk of the neck, ascending within the carotid sheath and dividing into the internal and external carotid arteries.
cards.att: The right arises from the brachiocephalic trunk behind the right sternoclavicular joint; the left arises directly from the arch of the aorta in the superior mediastinum. Both ascend in the carotid sheath and divide at the upper border of the thyroid cartilage, at the level of C4.
cards.sup: Gives no named branches in the neck; its terminal branches are the internal and external carotid arteries.
cards.act: Conveys blood to the head and neck.
cards.rel: Within the carotid sheath the internal jugular vein lies lateral and the vagus nerve posteriorly between them. Anteriorly the infrahyoid muscles and sternocleidomastoid; posteriorly the transverse processes, sympathetic trunk and the anterior tubercle of C6 (carotid tubercle of Chassaignac).
cards.clin: Compressed against the carotid tubercle of C6 to control bleeding. The carotid sinus, at the bifurcation, is a baroreceptor supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve; pressure on it can cause reflex bradycardia and syncope. The bifurcation is the usual site of atheromatous plaque and of endarterectomy.
cards.exam: Q. At what level does the common carotid artery divide? A. At the upper border of the thyroid cartilage, level with the C4 vertebra.

cards.desc: A fibrous ring at the apex of the orbit that surrounds the optic canal and the medial part of the superior orbital fissure and gives origin to the four recti.
cards.att: Attached to the body of the sphenoid around the margins of the optic canal and to the lower margin of the superior orbital fissure, including the infra-optic tubercle and the spina recti lateralis on the greater wing. From it arise superior, inferior, medial and lateral recti.
cards.act: Provides a common fixed posterior origin for the four recti, so their pull is directed from the orbital apex to the globe.
cards.rel: Passing through the ring: optic nerve with the ophthalmic artery, the superior and inferior divisions of the oculomotor nerve, the nasociliary nerve and the abducent nerve. Passing through the superior orbital fissure outside the ring: lacrimal, frontal and trochlear nerves and the superior ophthalmic vein.
cards.clin: The anatomical basis of the retrobulbar block, where anaesthetic is placed within the muscle cone. Lesions at the orbital apex involving the ring produce total ophthalmoplegia with visual loss, while a lesion of the superior orbital fissure alone spares vision. Pain on eye movement in retrobulbar neuritis arises because the optic nerve sheath is tethered to the ring.
cards.exam: Q. Which structures enter the orbit through the superior orbital fissure outside the common tendinous ring? A. The lacrimal, frontal and trochlear nerves and the superior ophthalmic vein.

cards.desc: The transparent, avascular anterior one-sixth of the fibrous coat of the eyeball, more curved than the sclera and the eye's principal refracting surface.
cards.att: Continuous with the sclera at the limbus (corneoscleral junction). It has five layers from before backwards: corneal epithelium, anterior limiting lamina (Bowman's layer), substantia propria or stroma, posterior limiting lamina (Descemet's membrane) and the corneal endothelium.
cards.sup: Avascular; nourished by the aqueous humour, the tear film and the capillaries at the limbus. Sensory supply is by the long and short ciliary nerves, from the nasociliary branch of the ophthalmic nerve, CN V1.
cards.act: Provides about two-thirds of the refractive power of the eye and, with the sclera, protects the intra-ocular contents.
cards.rel: Bounded in front by the tear film and precorneal conjunctival epithelium, behind by the aqueous humour of the anterior chamber; the iris lies behind it across the anterior chamber, and the limbus surrounds it.
cards.clin: Its dense sensory innervation makes corneal abrasion intensely painful and provides the corneal reflex, afferent V1 and efferent facial nerve. Being avascular and immunologically privileged, it is the most successfully transplanted tissue. A Kayser-Fleischer ring at the periphery of Descemet's membrane indicates Wilson's disease.
cards.exam: Q. Name the five layers of the cornea from anterior to posterior. A. Epithelium, Bowman's layer, stroma, Descemet's membrane, endothelium.

cards.desc: The only complete cartilaginous ring in the airway, shaped like a signet ring at the lower end of the larynx at the level of the C6 vertebra.
cards.att: A narrow anterior arch and a broad posterior lamina. Articulates above with the inferior horns of the thyroid cartilage and with the bases of the arytenoids at synovial joints. Gives attachment to cricothyroid and posterior and lateral cricoarytenoid muscles, the conus elasticus, the cricopharyngeus, the cricotracheal ligament and the longitudinal muscle of the oesophagus.
cards.sup: Cricothyroid and inferior laryngeal branches of the superior and inferior thyroid arteries.
cards.act: Supports the larynx and holds the airway open; its joints with the thyroid cartilage and arytenoids provide the mechanism for tensing and for abducting and adducting the vocal folds.
cards.rel: Marks the level of C6, where the pharynx becomes oesophagus, the larynx becomes trachea, the middle thyroid vein and inferior thyroid artery are encountered, and the carotid tubercle can be palpated. The isthmus of the thyroid lies just below it.
cards.clin: Backward pressure on the cricoid (Sellick manoeuvre) compresses the oesophagus against the vertebral body during rapid sequence induction. Being a complete ring, the subglottis is the narrowest part of the infant airway, so a tight tube causes subglottic stenosis. Emergency airway access is made through the cricothyroid membrane just above it.
cards.exam: Q. What is anatomically unique about the cricoid cartilage and why does it matter? A. It is the only complete ring in the airway, which allows cricoid pressure to occlude the oesophagus and makes the subglottis the narrowest part of the child's airway.

cards.desc: A two-bellied suprahyoid muscle slung from the mastoid region to the mandible, defining the digastric (submandibular) triangle of the neck.
cards.att: Posterior belly arises from the mastoid notch on the medial side of the mastoid process; anterior belly arises from the digastric fossa on the inner surface of the lower border of the mandible near the symphysis. The two join in an intermediate tendon which perforates stylohyoid and is held to the body and greater cornu of the hyoid by a fibrous sling.
cards.sup: Anterior belly by the nerve to mylohyoid from the inferior alveolar branch of the mandibular nerve; posterior belly by the digastric branch of the facial nerve. Arteries: facial and occipital.
cards.act: Depresses the mandible and opens the mouth when the hyoid is fixed; elevates the hyoid in swallowing when the mandible is fixed.
cards.rel: Posterior belly crosses superficial to the internal and external carotid arteries, the internal jugular vein, and the hypoglossal, vagus and accessory nerves, and marks the upper limit of the carotid dissection. The submandibular gland lies within the triangle bounded by the two bellies and the lower border of the mandible.
cards.clin: The posterior belly is the key surgical landmark of the upper neck, guiding the surgeon to the carotid vessels, the hypoglossal nerve and the facial nerve trunk. Its two bellies have different nerve supplies because they develop from the first and second pharyngeal arches respectively.
cards.exam: Q. Why do the two bellies of digastric have different nerve supplies? A. The anterior belly is first arch (mandibular nerve) and the posterior belly is second arch (facial nerve) in origin.

cards.desc: Light, cuboidal midline bone of the cranial base lying between the two orbits and forming the roof and much of the lateral wall of the nasal cavity.
cards.att: Has a horizontal cribriform plate with the crista galli projecting above for the falx cerebri, a vertical perpendicular plate forming the upper part of the nasal septum, and two lateral labyrinths containing the ethmoidal air cells and bearing the superior and middle nasal conchae. Its lateral surface, the lamina papyracea, forms most of the medial wall of the orbit. Articulates with the frontal, sphenoid, nasal, lacrimal, maxillary, palatine and vomer bones and the inferior conchae.
cards.sup: Anterior and posterior ethmoidal branches of the ophthalmic artery and sphenopalatine branches; the cribriform plate transmits the olfactory nerve filaments.
cards.act: Separates the nasal cavity from the anterior cranial fossa and the orbits, supports the conchae that condition inspired air, and transmits the olfactory nerves.
cards.rel: Olfactory bulbs rest on the cribriform plate above; the orbit lies lateral to the lamina papyracea; the sphenoid sinus lies behind and the frontal sinus in front and above.
cards.clin: Fracture of the cribriform plate tears the meninges and causes CSF rhinorrhoea and anosmia, with a risk of meningitis. Ethmoid sinusitis spreads through the paper-thin lamina papyracea to cause orbital cellulitis, the commonest cause of orbital cellulitis in children.
cards.exam: Q. Which part of the ethmoid separates the ethmoidal air cells from the orbit and why is it important? A. The lamina papyracea, so thin that ethmoid sinus infection readily spreads to produce orbital cellulitis.

cards.desc: The auricle and the external acoustic meatus, ending medially at the tympanic membrane.
cards.att: The auricle has a framework of elastic cartilage covered by adherent skin, except the fibrofatty lobule. The external acoustic meatus is about 24 mm long and S-shaped: the outer one-third is cartilaginous, the inner two-thirds bony in the temporal bone, and the whole is closed medially by the tympanic membrane.
cards.sup: Sensory supply from the great auricular and lesser occipital nerves (cervical plexus), the auriculotemporal nerve (CN V3), the auricular branch of the vagus (CN X), and a contribution from the facial nerve. Arterial supply from the posterior auricular and superficial temporal arteries and the deep auricular branch of the maxillary artery.
cards.act: Collects and channels sound to the tympanic membrane and helps localise sound.
cards.rel: The parotid gland lies anterior and inferior to the meatus, the mastoid process posterior, and the temporomandibular joint immediately in front of its cartilaginous part; the middle cranial fossa lies above the bony meatus.
cards.clin: To straighten the meatus for otoscopy, pull the auricle upwards, backwards and laterally in an adult, and downwards and backwards in an infant. Stimulating the auricular branch of the vagus in the meatus provokes Arnold's cough reflex, and a furuncle in the cartilaginous part is exquisitely painful because the skin is bound down.
cards.exam: Q. Which nerve mediates the cough reflex on cleaning the external acoustic meatus? A. The auricular branch of the vagus, Arnold's nerve.

cards.desc: A thick fibrous band bridging the concavity of the carpus and converting the carpal arch into the carpal tunnel.
cards.att: Attached medially to the pisiform and the hook of the hamate, and laterally to the tubercle of the scaphoid and the ridge of the trapezium; continuous above with the deep fascia of the forearm and below with the palmar aponeurosis.
cards.act: Holds the long flexor tendons against the carpus, preventing bowstringing during wrist flexion, and gives origin to the thenar and hypothenar muscles.
cards.rel: Deep to it in the carpal tunnel run the median nerve and nine tendons: four of flexor digitorum superficialis, four of flexor digitorum profundus and one of flexor pollicis longus. Superficial to it pass the ulnar nerve and artery in the canal of Guyon, the palmar cutaneous branches of the median and ulnar nerves, and the tendon of palmaris longus, which is partly inserted into it.
cards.clin: Thickening or a reduction in tunnel volume compresses the median nerve, causing carpal tunnel syndrome with paraesthesia of the lateral three and a half digits and thenar wasting; sensation over the thenar eminence is spared because the palmar cutaneous branch passes superficial to the retinaculum. Surgical release divides the retinaculum.
cards.exam: Q. Why is thenar skin sensation preserved in carpal tunnel syndrome? A. The palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve arises proximally and crosses superficial to the flexor retinaculum.

cards.desc: Unpaired bone forming the forehead, the roofs of the orbits and the floor of the anterior cranial fossa.
cards.att: Has a squamous part with the glabella, superciliary arches and frontal eminences, two orbital plates and a nasal part. Bears the supraorbital margin with a supraorbital notch or foramen, the frontal crest and foramen caecum internally, the lacrimal fossa laterally in the orbital plate and the trochlear fovea medially, and encloses the frontal sinuses. Articulates with the parietals at the coronal suture, and with the sphenoid, ethmoid, nasal, lacrimal, maxillary and zygomatic bones.
cards.sup: Supraorbital and supratrochlear branches of the ophthalmic artery and the middle meningeal artery internally; sensory supply of the overlying skin and sinus by the supraorbital and supratrochlear nerves (V1).
cards.act: Protects the frontal lobes, roofs the orbit, and its air sinuses lighten the skull and add resonance to the voice.
cards.rel: Frontal lobes and the falx attachment lie on its internal surface, the orbital contents and the lacrimal gland below the orbital plate, and the frontal sinus drains into the middle meatus through the frontonasal duct and ethmoidal infundibulum.
cards.clin: Persistence of the metopic suture in the adult can be mistaken for a fracture. The supraorbital nerve is blocked at the supraorbital notch, palpable at the junction of the medial third and lateral two thirds of the supraorbital margin. Frontal sinusitis causes tenderness over the floor of the sinus and can spread to the meninges.
cards.exam: Q. What is the metopic suture? A. The persistent midline frontal suture between the two halves of the frontal bone, normally obliterated by about the sixth year.

cards.desc: The largest branch of the ophthalmic nerve, running forwards on the roof of the orbit just beneath the periorbita.
cards.att: Arises from the ophthalmic nerve in the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus, enters the orbit through the superior orbital fissure outside the common tendinous ring, runs forward on the upper surface of levator palpebrae superioris, and divides about halfway into the supra-orbital and supratrochlear nerves.
cards.act: Sensory to the forehead and scalp as far back as the vertex, the upper eyelid and conjunctiva, and the mucosa of the frontal sinus.
cards.rel: Lies between levator palpebrae superioris below and the periorbita of the orbital roof above; the trochlear nerve lies medial to it as both enter the fissure, and the lacrimal nerve lies lateral.
cards.clin: Its position immediately under the orbital roof makes it the nerve reached by a subperiosteal approach to the superior orbit, and pain over the forehead in frontal sinusitis is referred along it.
cards.exam: Q. Which three nerves enter the orbit through the superior orbital fissure outside the common tendinous ring? A. The lacrimal, frontal and trochlear nerves.

cards.desc: One of the two terminal branches of the abdominal aorta, running from the aortic bifurcation to the pelvic brim.
cards.att: Arises at the bifurcation of the abdominal aorta at the level of the fourth lumbar vertebra, a little to the left of the midline; passes inferolaterally along the medial border of psoas major for about 5 cm and divides in front of the sacroiliac joint into external and internal iliac arteries. It normally gives only small branches to peritoneum, psoas, ureter and surrounding tissue.
cards.act: Conveys the whole arterial supply of the pelvis, perineum and lower limb.
cards.rel: The ureter crosses the bifurcation anteriorly, and on the left the superior rectal vessels and the apex of the sigmoid mesocolon lie in front; the right common iliac artery crosses in front of the left common iliac vein and the beginning of the inferior vena cava; the sympathetic trunk, obturator nerve and lumbosacral trunk lie behind.
cards.clin: Aorto-iliac occlusive disease gives Leriche syndrome: buttock and thigh claudication, absent femoral pulses and impotence. The ureter crossing the bifurcation is the standard landmark for identifying it at pelvic surgery, and the site where a ureteric calculus commonly lodges.
cards.exam: Q. At what vertebral level does the aorta divide into common iliac arteries? A. The lower border of the fourth lumbar vertebra.

cards.desc: Paired dorsolateral erectile columns of the penis, each beginning as a crus attached to the ischiopubic ramus and running forward to form the bulk of the body.
cards.att: Proximally each crus is attached to the ischiopubic ramus and covered by ischiocavernosus; the two bodies meet under the pubic symphysis, are bound by tunica albuginea and an incomplete median septum (pectiniform), and end blunted beneath the glans.
cards.sup: Deep artery of the penis (from the internal pudendal) with helicine branches; drainage via deep dorsal vein to the prostatic venous plexus. Cavernous nerves from the prostatic plexus (parasympathetic S2, S3, S4) mediate erection.
cards.act: Engorgement of its cavernous spaces against the rigid tunica albuginea produces penile rigidity in erection.
cards.rel: Lies dorsal to the corpus spongiosum, deep to the deep fascia of the penis (Buck fascia); the deep dorsal vein, dorsal arteries and dorsal nerves lie in the dorsal groove between the two bodies.
cards.clin: Site of needle aspiration and intracavernosal injection in priapism and erectile dysfunction. Fibrous plaques of the tunica albuginea cause Peyronie disease; tearing of the tunica during intercourse is penile fracture.
cards.exam: Q. Which artery fills the corpus cavernosum during erection? A. The deep artery of the penis, a branch of the internal pudendal artery.

cards.desc: Single ventral (median) erectile column that transmits the spongy urethra, expanded proximally as the bulb of the penis and distally as the glans.
cards.att: The bulb is attached to the inferior surface of the perineal membrane and covered by bulbospongiosus; the body lies in the ventral groove between the corpora cavernosa and expands distally into the glans penis.
cards.sup: Artery of the bulb of the penis and the urethral artery, both from the internal pudendal artery; venous drainage to the deep dorsal vein and prostatic venous plexus.
cards.act: Remains less turgid than the corpora cavernosa during erection, so the spongy urethra stays patent for ejaculation.
cards.rel: Ventral to the corpora cavernosa; the spongy urethra runs through its length. The bulbourethral (Cowper) glands open into the urethra within the bulb.
cards.clin: Straddle injury ruptures the bulb, and urine and blood extravasate into the superficial perineal pouch, spreading into the scrotum and anterior abdominal wall deep to Scarpa fascia but not into the thigh.
cards.exam: Q. Why does the urethra remain patent during erection? A. It runs in the corpus spongiosum, which has a thinner tunica and stays less turgid than the corpora cavernosa.

cards.desc: Thick-walled muscular tube about 45 cm long conveying sperm from the tail of the epididymis to the ejaculatory duct behind the bladder.
cards.att: Begins at the tail of the epididymis, ascends in the spermatic cord, traverses the inguinal canal, hooks around the inferior epigastric artery at the deep ring, crosses the ureter near the ischial spine, dilates as the ampulla behind the bladder and joins the duct of the seminal vesicle to form the ejaculatory duct.
cards.sup: Artery to the ductus deferens, usually from the superior vesical artery; sympathetic fibres from the hypogastric plexus (L1, L2) drive its peristalsis.
cards.act: Thick three-layered smooth muscle propels sperm rapidly to the prostatic urethra during emission.
cards.rel: In the spermatic cord it is the firm cord-like structure felt posteriorly. In the pelvis it crosses superior to the ureter, the classic "water under the bridge" relation, and lies medial to the seminal vesicle.
cards.clin: Divided and ligated at vasectomy through a scrotal incision. Congenital bilateral absence of the vas is associated with cystic fibrosis mutations; a beaded, thickened vas suggests genital tuberculosis.
cards.exam: Q. What is the relation of the ductus deferens to the ureter? A. The ductus crosses superior (anterior) to the ureter, water under the bridge.

cards.desc: The voluntary striated muscle that surrounds the whole length of the anal canal outside the internal sphincter.
cards.att: Described in subcutaneous, superficial and deep parts. The subcutaneous part encircles the anal orifice with no bony attachment; the superficial part is attached in front to the perineal body and behind to the coccyx through the anococcygeal ligament; the deep part is a thick ring blending above with puborectalis.
cards.sup: Inferior rectal branch of the pudendal nerve (S2, S3), with a contribution from the perineal branch of the fourth sacral nerve.
cards.act: Voluntary closure of the anal canal; it maintains tonic contraction at rest and contracts strongly to defer defaecation, relaxing during defaecation.
cards.rel: Separated from the internal anal sphincter by the intersphincteric plane containing the longitudinal muscle layer; the ischio-anal fossa with its fat and the inferior rectal vessels and nerve lies lateral; the anococcygeal body behind and the perineal body in front.
cards.clin: Obstetric injury tearing the external sphincter is a third degree perineal tear, and extension into the anal mucosa is a fourth degree tear; unrepaired, it causes faecal incontinence. Fistula-in-ano is classified by Parks according to its course relative to this sphincter, and division of the deep part or puborectalis in fistula surgery causes incontinence.
cards.exam: Q. What is the nerve supply of the external anal sphincter? A. The inferior rectal branch of the pudendal nerve, S2 and S3, with the perineal branch of S4.

cards.desc: The larger terminal branch of the common iliac artery, running along the pelvic brim to become the femoral artery.
cards.att: Begins in front of the sacroiliac joint, runs downwards and laterally along the medial border of psoas major on the pelvic brim, and passes behind the inguinal ligament at the midinguinal point to become the femoral artery. Branches: inferior epigastric and deep circumflex iliac arteries, both arising just above the inguinal ligament.
cards.act: Principal arterial supply of the lower limb, with branches to the anterior abdominal wall.
cards.rel: Accompanied medially by the external iliac vein; crossed at its origin by the ureter (left) and by the ductus deferens or the round ligament and ovarian vessels; the genitofemoral nerve lies lateral, testicular vessels cross in front; the deep circumflex iliac vein crosses in front of it.
cards.clin: The inferior epigastric artery is the landmark dividing indirect hernias, whose sac lies lateral to it, from direct hernias, which bulge medial to it. The external iliac artery is the usual site of anastomosis of the renal artery in a transplant.
cards.exam: Q. Where does the external iliac artery become the femoral artery? A. Behind the inguinal ligament at the midinguinal point, midway between the anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic symphysis.

cards.desc: Large irregular bone of the pelvic girdle formed by fusion of the ilium, ischium and pubis, meeting the sacrum behind and its fellow in front.
cards.att: The three parts fuse at the triradiate cartilage in the acetabulum in the mid-teens. Articulations: with the sacrum at the sacroiliac joint, with the head of the femur at the hip joint, and with the opposite hip bone at the pubic symphysis. Landmarks: iliac crest, anterior and posterior superior and inferior iliac spines, greater and lesser sciatic notches, ischial spine and tuberosity, obturator foramen, acetabulum with its notch, pubic tubercle, pecten pubis and iliopubic eminence.
cards.act: Transmits body weight from the vertebral column to the lower limb in standing and to the ischial tuberosities in sitting; gives attachment to abdominal wall, gluteal, hamstring, adductor and pelvic floor muscles.
cards.rel: The greater sciatic foramen transmits the piriformis, superior and inferior gluteal vessels and nerves, sciatic nerve, pudendal nerve and internal pudendal vessels; the lesser sciatic foramen transmits the tendon of obturator internus and the pudendal nerve and vessels re-entering the perineum.
cards.clin: The anterior superior iliac spine and pubic tubercle are the ends of the inguinal ligament and standard surface landmarks. The iliac crest is used for bone marrow aspiration and as a bone graft donor site. The ischial spine, palpable per vaginam, guides pudendal nerve block.
cards.exam: Q. At what site and age do the three parts of the hip bone fuse? A. At the triradiate cartilage in the acetabulum, around 15 to 17 years.

cards.desc: The medial terminal branch of the common iliac artery, the main artery of the pelvis, perineum and gluteal region.
cards.att: Arises in front of the sacroiliac joint, descends about 4 cm to the upper border of the greater sciatic foramen, and divides into anterior and posterior divisions. Anterior division: superior vesical (from the patent proximal part of the umbilical artery), inferior vesical (in the female the vaginal artery), middle rectal, uterine, obturator, internal pudendal and inferior gluteal. Posterior division: iliolumbar, lateral sacral and superior gluteal.
cards.act: Supplies the pelvic viscera, pelvic walls, perineum, external genitalia and the gluteal region.
cards.rel: The ureter descends in front of it and the internal iliac vein and lumbosacral trunk lie behind; the external iliac vein lies anterolateral above, and the obturator nerve runs below and lateral on the pelvic wall.
cards.clin: Bilateral internal iliac ligation or embolisation is used for uncontrollable postpartum or pelvic fracture haemorrhage; collateral flow keeps the pelvis viable. The obliterated umbilical artery persists as the medial umbilical ligament.
cards.exam: Q. Name the three branches of the posterior division of the internal iliac artery. A. Iliolumbar, lateral sacral and superior gluteal.

cards.desc: Walnut-sized fibromuscular and glandular organ lying below the bladder neck and in front of the rectum, surrounding the prostatic urethra.
cards.att: Base fused with the bladder neck above, apex resting on the perineal membrane below; anterior, posterior and two inferolateral surfaces. Zones: peripheral, central, transition and anterior fibromuscular stroma; the median sulcus divides the posterior surface.
cards.sup: Arteries: inferior vesical, middle rectal and internal pudendal. Veins: prostatic venous plexus draining to the internal iliac veins and communicating with the internal vertebral venous plexus. Nerves: inferior hypogastric (pelvic) plexus. Lymph: internal iliac and sacral nodes.
cards.act: Secretes thin alkaline fluid rich in citric acid, zinc and prostate specific antigen, contributing about 30 per cent of the ejaculate and liquefying the semen.
cards.rel: Bladder above, rectum behind separated by the rectovesical fascia of Denonvilliers, levator ani inferolaterally, retropubic space of Retzius and pubic symphysis in front. Ejaculatory ducts pierce the posterior surface and open at the seminal colliculus.
