cards.clin: Benign hyperplasia begins in the transition zone and obstructs the urethra; carcinoma arises mainly in the peripheral zone, hardening the posterior surface and obliterating the median sulcus on digital rectal examination. Spread to the vertebrae and skull occurs through the valveless prostatic and vertebral venous plexuses (Batson).
cards.exam: Q. Which zone gives rise to benign prostatic hyperplasia and which to carcinoma? A. Transition zone for hyperplasia, peripheral zone for carcinoma.

cards.desc: U-shaped muscular sling of levator ani that loops behind the anorectal junction, the most medial and inferior part of the muscle.
cards.att: Origin: posterior surface of the body of the pubis on each side, close to the symphysis. Insertion: none bony; the two sides unite behind the anorectal junction as a continuous sling blending with the deep part of the external anal sphincter.
cards.sup: Nerve to levator ani (anterior ramus of S4) and the inferior rectal branch of the pudendal nerve (S2, S3, S4).
cards.act: Pulls the anorectal junction forwards to maintain the anorectal angle of about 80 to 90 degrees, the principal mechanism of faecal continence; it relaxes to straighten the angle during defaecation.
cards.rel: Lies immediately above the deep part of the external anal sphincter, behind the perineal body and prostate or vagina; the anorectal junction and anal canal pass through the sling.
cards.clin: Palpable as a firm posterior shelf on digital rectal examination. Failure of relaxation (anismus, paradoxical contraction) causes obstructed defaecation; division of the sling in fistula surgery causes faecal incontinence.
cards.exam: Q. Which muscle maintains the anorectal angle? A. Puborectalis, the U-shaped sling of levator ani around the anorectal junction.

cards.desc: The terminal 12 cm of the large intestine, continuing the sigmoid colon in front of the third sacral vertebra and ending at the anorectal junction.
cards.att: Follows the curve of the sacrum and coccyx (sacral flexure), then turns sharply backwards at the anorectal junction 2 to 3 cm in front of and below the tip of the coccyx as it pierces the pelvic diaphragm. It has no mesentery, taeniae coli, sacculations or appendices epiploicae; three transverse rectal folds (valves of Houston) indent the lumen. Peritoneum covers the front and sides of the upper third, the front only of the middle third, and none of the lower third.
cards.sup: Arteries: superior rectal from the inferior mesenteric, middle rectal from the internal iliac and inferior rectal from the internal pudendal. Veins: superior rectal to the portal system, middle and inferior rectal to the systemic system. Lymphatics: from the upper part along the superior rectal vessels to inferior mesenteric nodes, from the lower part to internal iliac nodes. Nerves: sympathetic from the inferior hypogastric plexus, parasympathetic from the pelvic splanchnic nerves S2, S3 and S4.
cards.act: Stores faeces; distension initiates the defaecation reflex with reflex relaxation of the internal anal sphincter.
cards.rel: Behind lie the sacrum, coccyx, piriformis, the sacral plexus and the median sacral vessels; in front in the male the rectovesical pouch, base of the bladder, seminal vesicles, ductus deferens and prostate; in the female the rectouterine pouch of Douglas, vagina and cervix. The ampulla rests on the levator ani.
cards.clin: The prostate, cervix and pouch of Douglas are palpable on digital rectal examination, so pelvic abscess and peritoneal deposits can be felt. Rectal carcinoma is staged by the peritoneal reflection and the mesorectal fascia; total mesorectal excision follows this plane while preserving the hypogastric nerves to avoid impotence.
cards.exam: Q. At what level does the rectum begin and end? A. It begins in front of the third sacral vertebra and ends at the anorectal junction, 2 to 3 cm in front of and below the tip of the coccyx.

cards.desc: Large triangular bone formed by fusion of the five sacral vertebrae, wedged between the two hip bones to complete the posterior wall of the pelvis.
cards.att: Base above bears the promontory, the superior articular processes for L5 and the alae; the apex below articulates with the coccyx. Articulations: L5 above, coccyx below, and the ilium on each side at the auricular surface. Features: four pairs of anterior and posterior sacral foramina, median, intermediate and lateral sacral crests, sacral canal, sacral hiatus and cornua.
cards.act: Transmits body weight from the vertebral column to the pelvic girdle and forms the posterior wall of the pelvic cavity; anchors the sacrotuberous and sacrospinous ligaments.
cards.rel: Anteriorly the sigmoid colon, rectum, superior rectal vessels and the sympathetic trunks with the median sacral vessels; the sacral plexus lies on piriformis in front of the anterior foramina. The dural sac ends at the level of S2.
cards.clin: Caudal epidural anaesthesia is given through the sacral hiatus between the sacral cornua. The sacral promontory is the landmark for measuring the obstetric conjugate and for pelvic inlet assessment. Sacralisation of L5 and lumbarisation of S1 are common variants.
cards.exam: Q. At what vertebral level does the dural sac end in the adult? A. The lower border of S2, marked on the sacrum.

cards.desc: Paired oval male gonad suspended in the scrotum by the spermatic cord, producing spermatozoa and testosterone.
cards.att: Enclosed in the tough tunica albuginea, which sends septa from the mediastinum testis dividing it into about 250 lobules of seminiferous tubules; tubules drain through the rete testis and efferent ductules into the head of the epididymis. The tunica vaginalis covers all but the posterior bare area.
cards.sup: Testicular artery from the abdominal aorta at L2; veins form the pampiniform plexus, the right testicular vein draining into the inferior vena cava and the left into the left renal vein. Nerves from the T10 sympathetic segment via the renal and aortic plexuses. Lymph drains to the para-aortic (lumbar) nodes at L2.
cards.act: Spermatogenesis in the seminiferous tubules; testosterone secretion by interstitial (Leydig) cells.
cards.rel: Epididymis posterolateral, spermatic cord above, tunica vaginalis in front and at the sides; the scrotal skin and dartos are superficial.
cards.clin: Testicular pain is referred to the periumbilical region because of the T10 supply. Torsion occurs with a bell-clapper deformity and demands surgery within six hours. Varicocele is far commoner on the left, where the testicular vein joins the left renal vein at a right angle. Testicular tumours spread to para-aortic nodes, while scrotal skin drains to superficial inguinal nodes.
cards.exam: Q. To which lymph nodes does the testis drain? A. Para-aortic (lumbar) nodes at L2, following its embryological origin, not the inguinal nodes.

cards.desc: Muscular tube about 18 to 20 cm long carrying urine and semen from the internal urethral orifice of the bladder to the external urethral orifice on the glans penis.
cards.att: Four parts: preprostatic (intramural), prostatic, membranous and spongy. The prostatic part is the widest and bears the urethral crest, seminal colliculus with the prostatic utricle and ejaculatory duct openings, and the prostatic sinuses. The membranous part traverses the deep perineal pouch and perineal membrane, encircled by the external urethral sphincter. The spongy part runs in the corpus spongiosum, dilated in the bulb and as the navicular fossa in the glans.
cards.sup: Arteries: inferior vesical, middle rectal and internal pudendal branches (urethral and bulbar arteries). Nerves: prostatic plexus and the dorsal nerve of the penis (pudendal, S2, S3, S4).
cards.act: Conducts urine during micturition and semen during ejaculation; the internal sphincter at the bladder neck closes during ejaculation to prevent retrograde flow.
cards.rel: Prostatic part is surrounded by the prostate; membranous part lies between the prostatic apex and the bulb, with the bulbourethral glands lateral to it; spongy part lies within the corpus spongiosum with the bulbourethral ducts opening into it.
cards.clin: The external urethral orifice is the narrowest part and the membranous urethra the least dilatable, so a catheter that will pass the meatus will usually pass throughout. Straddle injury ruptures the bulbous urethra with extravasation into the superficial perineal pouch; pelvic fracture ruptures the membranous urethra with extravasation above the perineal membrane and a high-riding prostate.
cards.exam: Q. Which part of the male urethra is narrowest and which is least dilatable? A. The external urethral orifice is narrowest; the membranous part is least dilatable.

cards.desc: Distensible muscular reservoir for urine lying in the anterior part of the lesser pelvis behind the pubic symphysis when empty.
cards.att: Has an apex connected to the umbilicus by the median umbilical ligament (urachal remnant), a fundus (base) posteriorly, a body, and a neck resting on the prostate in the male and the pelvic fascia in the female. The trigone on the internal surface of the base is smooth and lies between the two ureteric orifices and the internal urethral orifice.
cards.sup: Arteries: superior and inferior vesical branches of the internal iliac artery (vaginal artery replacing the inferior vesical in the female). Veins: vesical venous plexus to the internal iliac veins. Nerves: parasympathetic pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2, S3, S4) motor to the detrusor, sympathetic from L1, L2 via the hypogastric plexuses, pain from the superior surface travelling with sympathetics and from the base with parasympathetics. Lymph: external and internal iliac nodes.
cards.act: Stores urine and expels it by detrusor contraction with relaxation of the sphincters during micturition.
cards.rel: Peritoneum covers the superior surface only; anteriorly the retropubic space of Retzius; posteriorly the rectovesical pouch, seminal vesicles and ductus deferens in the male, and the uterus and vagina in the female; below, the prostate or the pelvic floor.
cards.clin: A full bladder rises above the pubic symphysis and strips the peritoneum upward, allowing suprapubic puncture or catheterisation without entering the peritoneal cavity. Rupture of the distended dome is intraperitoneal, while rupture of the base with pelvic fracture is extraperitoneal. The trigone is derived from the mesonephric ducts and is the commonest site of cystoscopic pathology.
cards.exam: Q. What is the nerve supply of the detrusor muscle? A. Parasympathetic pelvic splanchnic nerves from S2, S3, S4.

cards.desc: A small triangular muscle forming the posterior part of the pelvic diaphragm, behind levator ani.
cards.att: Origin from the tip of the ischial spine by its apex; inserted by its base into the lateral margin of the coccyx and the lowest piece of the sacrum. It lies on the pelvic surface of the sacrospinous ligament and is coextensive with it.
cards.sup: Branches from the ventral rami of the fourth and fifth sacral nerves (S4, S5).
cards.act: Supports the pelvic viscera and pulls the coccyx forwards after it has been pushed back during defaecation or childbirth.
cards.rel: Levator ani lies in front, gluteus maximus and the sacrotuberous ligament behind the sacrospinous ligament; the pudendal nerve and internal pudendal vessels cross the ischial spine behind its origin; the greater sciatic foramen lies above and the lesser below.
cards.clin: Sacrospinous ligament fixation for vaginal vault prolapse places sutures through the coccygeus and ligament; the pudendal nerve and vessels and the sciatic nerve lie close to the ischial spine and are at risk. The ischial spine is also the landmark for pudendal nerve block in labour.
cards.exam: Q. What is the nerve supply of coccygeus? A. The ventral rami of the fourth and fifth sacral nerves.

cards.desc: The vein formed in front of the sacroiliac joint by the union of the external and internal iliac veins, ending by forming the inferior vena cava.
cards.att: Formed in front of the sacroiliac joint; the two veins ascend and unite at the level of the fifth lumbar vertebra to the right of the midline to form the inferior vena cava. The left vein is longer and more oblique and receives the median sacral vein; both receive iliolumbar and sometimes lateral sacral veins.
cards.act: Returns all venous blood from the lower limb, pelvis and perineum to the inferior vena cava.
cards.rel: The right common iliac artery crosses in front of the left common iliac vein; the right vein lies behind and then lateral to its own artery; the common iliac veins lie in front of the fifth lumbar vertebra and the sacral promontory.
cards.clin: May-Thurner (Cockett) syndrome: chronic compression of the left common iliac vein between the overlying right common iliac artery and the fifth lumbar vertebra causes left iliofemoral deep vein thrombosis and left leg swelling.
cards.exam: Q. Why is left leg deep vein thrombosis commoner than right? A. The left common iliac vein is compressed by the overlying right common iliac artery, May-Thurner syndrome.

cards.desc: Fibrocartilaginous secondary cartilaginous joint (symphysis) uniting adjacent vertebral bodies, from the C2/C3 to the L5/S1 level, twenty-three in all.
cards.att: Peripheral anulus fibrosus of concentric lamellae of fibrocartilage attached to the ring apophyses and blended with the anterior and posterior longitudinal ligaments, enclosing the gelatinous nucleus pulposus, a notochordal remnant; hyaline cartilage end-plates cover the vertebral surfaces.
cards.sup: Outer third of the anulus fibrosus is innervated by sinuvertebral (recurrent meningeal) nerves posteriorly and by grey rami communicantes laterally. The adult disc is avascular and is nourished by diffusion through the end-plates.
cards.act: Permits and limits movement between vertebrae, absorbs and distributes axial load; the discs together form about one quarter of the height of the presacral vertebral column.
cards.rel: Anteriorly the anterior longitudinal ligament, posteriorly the narrow posterior longitudinal ligament and the vertebral canal with the cord or cauda equina; the intervertebral foramina and their nerve roots lie posterolaterally.
cards.clin: The posterior longitudinal ligament is narrow in the lumbar region, so herniation of the nucleus pulposus occurs posterolaterally and compresses the traversing nerve root, one level below the named root of the exiting foramen. Disc height and water content fall with age, reducing stature.
cards.exam: Q. Why do disc herniations occur posterolaterally? A. The posterior longitudinal ligament is strong centrally but narrow laterally, so the anulus is weakest posterolaterally.

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned vessel and state the vertebral level at which it divides.
spotters.answer: Common iliac artery. It arises from the aortic bifurcation at L4 and divides in front of the sacroiliac joint at the level of L5 (lumbosacral disc) into external and internal iliac arteries. The ureter crosses the bifurcation anteriorly, the key landmark for finding the ureter at pelvic surgery.
spotters.followup: Which structure crosses the bifurcation of this vessel, and why does that matter in hysterectomy?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned artery and name its two divisions.
spotters.answer: Internal iliac artery (hypogastric artery). About 4 cm long, it begins at the L5 level anterior to the sacroiliac joint and divides at the upper border of the greater sciatic foramen into an anterior division (mainly visceral: superior and inferior vesical, middle rectal, uterine, internal pudendal, inferior gluteal, obturator, umbilical) and a posterior division (parietal: iliolumbar, lateral sacral, superior gluteal). It is the main supply to the pelvic viscera, perineum and gluteal region.
spotters.followup: Why does ligation of this artery for postpartum haemorrhage often fail to stop bleeding completely?

spotters.prompt: The pinned vessel is being traced towards the greater sciatic foramen. Identify it and name the branch that most commonly passes above piriformis.
spotters.answer: Internal iliac artery. Its posterior division gives the superior gluteal artery, which leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen above piriformis; the inferior gluteal artery from the anterior division leaves below piriformis. This above and below piriformis rule is the standard identification test in the gluteal region.
spotters.followup: Name three visceral branches of the anterior division of this artery.

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned artery and state what it becomes distally.
spotters.answer: External iliac artery. It runs along the medial border of psoas major on the pelvic brim and becomes the femoral artery as it passes deep to the inguinal ligament at the midinguinal point. Its two branches within the pelvis are the inferior epigastric and deep circumflex iliac arteries.
spotters.followup: Which branch of this artery forms the lateral boundary of the inguinal (Hesselbach) triangle?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned vessel and name the structure lying immediately medial to it behind the inguinal ligament.
spotters.answer: External iliac artery. Behind the inguinal ligament the external iliac vein lies medial to it, and the femoral canal with its lymph node lies medial to the vein. This lateral to medial order (artery, vein, canal) is the basis of the NAVEL mnemonic in the femoral triangle.
spotters.followup: Where would you palpate this vessel's continuation for a femoral pulse?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned vein and state where the two of them unite.
spotters.answer: Common iliac vein. Formed by union of the external and internal iliac veins in front of the sacroiliac joint, the right and left common iliac veins unite at the level of L5, to the right of the midline, to form the inferior vena cava. The left vein is longer and more horizontal and is crossed anteriorly by the right common iliac artery.
spotters.followup: Why is left leg deep vein thrombosis commoner than right (May-Thurner)?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned bone and state how many vertebrae fuse to form it.
spotters.answer: Sacrum. Five fused sacral vertebrae forming the wedge-shaped posterior wall of the pelvis. Its base carries the sacral promontory, its auricular surface articulates with the ilium at the sacroiliac joint, and four pairs of anterior and posterior sacral foramina transmit the sacral anterior and posterior rami.
spotters.followup: At what vertebral level does the dural sac normally end in the adult, and why does that matter for caudal anaesthesia?

spotters.prompt: The pin is on the lower posterior aspect of this bone at the deficient laminae. Identify the bone and name the aperture there.
spotters.answer: Sacrum. The gap is the sacral hiatus, formed by failure of fusion of the laminae of the fifth (and often fourth) sacral vertebra, bounded by the sacral cornua. It is the entry point for caudal epidural anaesthesia, widely used in paediatric and obstetric practice, since the dural sac ends higher at about S2.
spotters.followup: Which bony landmarks do you palpate to locate this aperture?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned bone and name its three constituent parts.
spotters.answer: Hip bone (os coxae). Ilium, ischium and pubis, fused at the acetabulum through the triradiate cartilage, which typically ossifies between about 15 and 25 years. The two hip bones with the sacrum and coccyx form the bony pelvis; the obturator foramen is closed by the obturator membrane except at the obturator canal.
spotters.followup: Which part of this bone bears weight in the sitting position?

spotters.prompt: The pin is on the sharp projection at the posterior margin of this bone separating the greater and lesser sciatic notches. Identify the bone and name that projection.
spotters.answer: Hip bone. The projection is the ischial spine, which separates the greater from the lesser sciatic notch and gives attachment to the sacrospinous ligament and to coccygeus. It is palpable per vaginam and is the landmark for a transvaginal pudendal nerve block, since the pudendal nerve hooks round it. It also defines station zero in obstetric assessment of fetal descent.
spotters.followup: Which ligament converts the lesser sciatic notch into a foramen?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned triangular muscle behind levator ani and state its attachments.
spotters.answer: Coccygeus (ischiococcygeus). It runs from the ischial spine to the lateral margin of the coccyx and lowest sacral segment, lying on the pelvic surface of the sacrospinous ligament, with which it is coextensive. With levator ani it completes the pelvic diaphragm and supports the pelvic viscera. Supplied by branches of the anterior rami of S4 and S5.
spotters.followup: Which ligament lies on the posterior surface of this muscle, and what foramen does that ligament help form?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned U-shaped sling at the anorectal junction and state its functional importance.
spotters.answer: Puborectalis. The medial, thickest part of levator ani, arising from the back of the pubic bodies and forming a sling behind the anorectal junction with no posterior bony attachment. It pulls the junction forwards, maintaining the anorectal angle of roughly 80 to 90 degrees, which is essential for faecal continence. With the deep external anal sphincter it forms the palpable anorectal ring; division of that ring in fistula surgery causes incontinence.
spotters.followup: Which fistula-in-ano operations risk dividing the anorectal ring, and what is the consequence?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned muscle surrounding the anal canal and state its nerve supply.
spotters.answer: External anal sphincter. Voluntary striated muscle in subcutaneous, superficial and deep parts, surrounding the whole length of the anal canal, supplied by the inferior rectal (inferior anal) branch of the pudendal nerve, S2 to S4. It is responsible for voluntary continence; the internal anal sphincter, in contrast, is smooth muscle under autonomic control and maintains resting tone.
spotters.followup: How would you distinguish this muscle from the internal anal sphincter on structure and control?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned muscle and name the fibromuscular mass into which its superficial fibres decussate anteriorly.
spotters.answer: External anal sphincter. Its superficial part is anchored anteriorly to the perineal body and posteriorly to the coccyx by the anococcygeal ligament. The perineal body is the central tendon of the perineum, the meeting point of the external anal sphincter, bulbospongiosus, both transverse perinei and levator ani fibres. Third and fourth degree obstetric tears through the perineal body into this sphincter cause faecal incontinence if not repaired.
spotters.followup: Which degrees of perineal tear involve this muscle, and how are they classified?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned viscus and state where it begins and ends.
spotters.answer: Rectum. About 12 to 15 cm long, it begins at the level of the S3 vertebra as the continuation of the sigmoid colon and ends at the anorectal junction, where it pierces the pelvic diaphragm to become the anal canal. Unlike the colon it has no taeniae coli, no sacculations and no appendices epiploicae, and it shows three transverse folds (valves of Houston).
spotters.followup: Name three features that distinguish this structure from sigmoid colon on inspection.

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned viscus and name its three arteries of supply.
spotters.answer: Rectum. Supplied by the superior rectal artery (continuation of the inferior mesenteric artery, the main supply), the middle rectal artery from the anterior division of the internal iliac artery, and the inferior rectal artery from the internal pudendal artery. Venous drainage is correspondingly portal above and systemic below, making the anorectal junction a site of portosystemic anastomosis, and it explains why rectal carcinoma metastasises to liver and lung.
spotters.followup: Explain why carcinoma of the lower part of this organ can metastasise to lung without passing through liver.

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned viscus and state the muscle that forms its wall and the nerve that makes it contract.
spotters.answer: Urinary bladder. Its wall is the detrusor muscle, smooth muscle supplied by parasympathetic fibres from the pelvic splanchnic nerves S2, S3 and S4, which contract the detrusor and relax the internal sphincter for micturition. In the adult the empty bladder lies entirely within the pelvis behind the pubic symphysis.
spotters.followup: Why can a full bladder be tapped suprapubically without entering the peritoneal cavity?

spotters.prompt: The pin is on the smooth triangular area on the internal aspect of the posterior wall of this organ. Identify the organ and name that area and its three corners.
spotters.answer: Urinary bladder. The area is the trigone, bounded by the two ureteric orifices and the internal urethral orifice, with the interureteric ridge running between the ureteric orifices. Its mucosa is smooth and firmly adherent (unlike the rugose remainder), it is mesodermal in origin from the absorbed mesonephric ducts, and it is highly sensitive, a common site for cystitis, tuberculous ulceration and tumour.
spotters.followup: Which part of this organ is covered by peritoneum, and where does urine collect when it ruptures there?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned gland and state its relations to bladder and urethra.
spotters.answer: Prostate. A fibromuscular glandular organ about the size of a chestnut (roughly 3 by 4 by 2 cm, 8 to 20 g), with its base fused to the neck of the bladder above and its apex resting on the external urethral sphincter below. The prostatic urethra runs through it, and the two ejaculatory ducts enter its posterosuperior aspect to open on the seminal colliculus.
spotters.followup: Which surface of this gland is palpated on digital rectal examination, and what feature is felt in the midline?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned gland and explain its route of metastasis to the vertebral column.
spotters.answer: Prostate. The prostatic venous plexus lies in the fascial sheath around the gland, receives the deep dorsal vein of the penis, drains to the internal iliac veins and communicates with the internal vertebral venous plexus (Batson plexus) through valveless connections. A rise in intra-abdominal pressure can therefore carry tumour emboli directly to the lumbar vertebrae, pelvis and skull, producing characteristically osteosclerotic (osteoblastic) secondaries.
spotters.followup: Which zone of this gland gives rise to most carcinomas, and which enlarges in benign hypertrophy?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned duct and state where it begins and ends.
spotters.answer: Deferent duct (ductus deferens, vas deferens). It begins at the tail of the epididymis, ascends in the spermatic cord through the inguinal canal, enters the pelvis at the deep inguinal ring, and ends by joining the duct of the seminal vesicle to form the ejaculatory duct. Its very thick smooth muscle wall gives it a characteristic whipcord feel on palpation in the scrotum, where it is divided at vasectomy.
spotters.followup: At vasectomy, where is this duct most conveniently approached and why?

spotters.prompt: The pin is on this duct in the pelvis, near the ischial spine. Identify it and state its relation to the ureter.
spotters.answer: Deferent duct. In the pelvis it crosses the ureter from lateral to medial, lying anterior and superior to it near the ischial spine, before reaching the base of the bladder and dilating as the ampulla. This is the male counterpart of the uterine artery and ureter relation, 'water under the bridge', and orientates the surgeon to the ureter in pelvic dissection.
spotters.followup: What is the female equivalent of this crossing relation, and why is it surgically important?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned organ and state its arterial supply.
spotters.answer: Testis. Supplied by the testicular artery, which arises directly from the abdominal aorta just below the renal artery at about L2, reflecting the organ's development on the posterior abdominal wall and its later descent. It is covered by the tunica albuginea and, anteriorly and laterally, the tunica vaginalis, a closed serous sac in which fluid collects as a hydrocele.
spotters.followup: Where do the veins draining this organ end on each side, and why is varicocele commoner on the left?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned organ and state its lymphatic drainage.
spotters.answer: Testis. Lymph drains along the testicular vessels to the para-aortic (lumbar) nodes at the L2 level, not to the inguinal nodes, because the organ develops on the posterior abdominal wall. Scrotal skin, by contrast, drains to the superficial inguinal nodes. Hence a testicular tumour is staged by abdominal imaging, while a scrotal skin lesion is assessed at the groin.
spotters.followup: A patient has an enlarged inguinal node and a testicular mass. What does that combination suggest anatomically?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned paired erectile body and state where its proximal end is attached.
spotters.answer: Corpus cavernosum of penis. The paired dorsal erectile bodies; each begins as a crus attached to the ischiopubic ramus and covered by ischiocavernosus, then the two run forward side by side enclosed in the tough tunica albuginea. The deep artery of the penis, a branch of the internal pudendal artery, runs within each and gives the helicine arteries responsible for erection.
spotters.followup: Which nerves mediate erection and which mediate emission, and where do they arise?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned single ventral erectile body and state what it transmits.
spotters.answer: Corpus spongiosum of penis. The single midline ventral erectile body, expanded proximally as the bulb of the penis (covered by bulbospongiosus) and distally as the glans. It transmits the spongy (penile) urethra throughout its length. Its tunica is thin and it stays at lower pressure during erection, so the urethra is not occluded and ejaculation can occur.
spotters.followup: Which muscle covers the proximal expansion of this body, and what is its action?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned tube and name its parts in the male.
spotters.answer: Urethra. In the male it is about 18 to 20 cm long with preprostatic, prostatic, membranous and spongy (penile) parts; the spongy part is often subdivided into bulbar and penile portions. In the female it is short, about 4 cm, running from the bladder neck to open in the vestibule anterior to the vaginal orifice, which explains the far higher incidence of ascending urinary infection in women.
spotters.followup: Which is the widest and most dilatable part, and which is the narrowest point in the male?

spotters.prompt: The pin is on the short segment of this tube passing through the perineal membrane. Identify the structure and state the injury pattern associated with this segment.
spotters.answer: Urethra, membranous part. About 1 to 2 cm long, it is the shortest and least dilatable part, surrounded by the external urethral sphincter (sphincter urethrae), supplied by the pudendal nerve, and fixed as it pierces the perineal membrane. Because it is fixed, it is the part torn in fractures of the pelvis, and extravasated urine collects in the deep perineal pouch or, with bladder neck disruption, above the perineal membrane. A straddle injury instead ruptures the bulbar spongy part, and urine then tracks into the superficial perineal pouch, scrotum, penis and anterior abdominal wall, but never into the thigh.
spotters.followup: Trace the path of extravasated urine after a straddle injury and state why it does not enter the thigh.

spotters.prompt: The pin is on the segment of this tube traversing the prostate. Identify the structure and name the elevation on which the ejaculatory ducts open.
spotters.answer: Urethra, prostatic part. The widest and most dilatable part, about 3 cm long, showing on its posterior wall the urethral crest with the seminal colliculus (verumontanum) in the middle. The prostatic utricle opens on the summit of the colliculus with an ejaculatory duct on either side, and the prostatic sinuses on each side of the crest receive the 20 to 30 prostatic ducts.
spotters.followup: What is the developmental origin of the prostatic utricle?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned gland and explain why its enlargement obstructs micturition.
spotters.answer: Prostate. Benign hyperplasia arises in the transition zone around the preprostatic and prostatic urethra, so the enlarging tissue compresses the urethral lumen and elevates the bladder neck, producing hesitancy, poor stream, terminal dribbling and eventually retention with detrusor hypertrophy and trabeculation. Carcinoma, in contrast, arises mostly in the peripheral zone, which is why it is felt as a hard nodule on rectal examination but often obstructs late.
spotters.followup: Why does the median lobe of this gland cause obstruction out of proportion to its size?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned muscle and state the two foramina its associated ligament helps to form.
spotters.answer: Coccygeus. It lies on the pelvic surface of the sacrospinous ligament, running from the ischial spine to the coccyx and lowest sacrum. The sacrospinous ligament converts the greater sciatic notch into the greater sciatic foramen and, with the sacrotuberous ligament, converts the lesser sciatic notch into the lesser sciatic foramen. The pudendal nerve crosses the ischial spine between the two ligaments, the site of the ischial spine pudendal block.
spotters.followup: Which nerve and vessels are at risk during a sacrospinous fixation for vault prolapse?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned vessel in the femoral triangle and state where you would palpate it in a shocked patient.
spotters.answer: Femoral artery. Continuation of the external iliac artery distal to the inguinal ligament, palpated at the mid-inguinal point, midway between the anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic symphysis. In the triangle it lies lateral to the femoral vein and medial to the femoral nerve, NAVEL from lateral to medial being nerve, artery, vein, empty space, lymphatics.
spotters.followup: Trace it distally: name the canal it enters and the opening through which it leaves the thigh.

spotters.prompt: Identify this vessel and state its relation to the artery beside it at the base of the femoral triangle.
spotters.answer: Femoral vein. Lies medial to the femoral artery at the inguinal ligament and posterior to it lower in the triangle. It is the continuation of the popliteal vein from the adductor hiatus and becomes the external iliac vein behind the inguinal ligament. Standard site for femoral central venous access, one finger medial to the palpable arterial pulse.
spotters.followup: Which two named tributaries join it within the femoral triangle?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned superficial vein and state the bony landmark used to find it at the ankle.
spotters.answer: Great saphenous vein. Constant position one centimetre anterior to the medial malleolus, the classic venous cut-down site. It ascends on the medial leg and thigh and drains into the femoral vein at the saphenous opening, roughly four centimetres inferolateral to the pubic tubercle. Accompanied by the saphenous nerve below the knee, so a cut-down risks saphenous neuralgia.
spotters.followup: Why is this the vein of choice for coronary artery bypass grafting, and which way must the graft be oriented?
spotters.sub: Superficial veins, medial leg and thigh

spotters.prompt: Identify this adductor and state which border of the femoral triangle its medial edge forms.
spotters.answer: Adductor longus. Anterior division of the obturator nerve, L2 to L4. Arises by a narrow tendon from the body of the pubis below the pubic crest and fans out into the middle third of the linea aspera. Its medial border forms the medial boundary of the femoral triangle, and it is the most anterior adductor, easily made prominent by resisted adduction. Common site of adductor strain, or rider's sprain.
spotters.followup: Which structure lies immediately deep to it, and what nerve divisions straddle that structure?

spotters.prompt: Identify this large composite muscle and account for its double nerve supply.
spotters.answer: Adductor magnus. Composite muscle with two parts. The adductor part, from the ischiopubic ramus to the linea aspera, is supplied by the posterior division of the obturator nerve. The hamstring part, from the ischial tuberosity to the adductor tubercle, is supplied by the tibial division of the sciatic nerve. The gap between the aponeurotic insertion and the adductor tubercle is the adductor hiatus, transmitting the femoral vessels into the popliteal fossa.
spotters.followup: Name the openings in this muscle and state what passes through each.

spotters.prompt: Identify this muscle and give its nerve supply and principal action.
spotters.answer: Gluteus maximus. Inferior gluteal nerve, L5, S1 and S2. Coarse-fibred, quadrilateral muscle from the posterior gluteal line of the ilium, sacrum, coccyx and sacrotuberous ligament, inserting mostly into the iliotibial tract with a deeper quarter into the gluteal tuberosity. Chief extensor and lateral rotator of the hip, recruited for rising from sitting, climbing stairs and running, not for ordinary level walking.
spotters.followup: Which quadrant of the buttock is safe for intramuscular injection and which nerve is at risk if you inject elsewhere?

spotters.prompt: Identify this muscle and state the clinical sign produced by its paralysis.
spotters.answer: Gluteus medius. Superior gluteal nerve, L4, L5 and S1. Runs from the outer ilium between the posterior and anterior gluteal lines to the lateral surface of the greater trochanter. With gluteus minimus it abducts the hip and, critically, holds the pelvis level on the stance side during walking. Paralysis gives a positive Trendelenburg sign: the pelvis drops on the unsupported swing side when the patient stands on the affected leg.
spotters.followup: Name three causes of a positive Trendelenburg sign other than nerve injury.

spotters.prompt: Identify this tendon, name the muscles contributing to it, and give one clinical test for its rupture.
spotters.answer: Calcaneal tendon, the tendo Achillis. Formed by gastrocnemius and soleus, inserting into the middle of the posterior surface of the calcaneal tuberosity with a retrocalcaneal bursa between it and the upper part of the bone. Thickest and strongest tendon in the body. Rupture, typically two to six centimetres above the insertion in a relatively avascular zone, gives a palpable gap, weak plantar flexion and a positive Simmonds or Thompson test, in which squeezing the calf fails to plantar flex the foot.
spotters.followup: Which nerve root value is tested by the ankle jerk transmitted through this tendon?

spotters.prompt: Identify this tendon and state which vessel is found alongside it at the ankle.
spotters.answer: Extensor hallucis longus. Deep fibular nerve, L5 and S1. Arises from the middle half of the medial surface of the fibula and the interosseous membrane, emerges between tibialis anterior and extensor digitorum longus, and inserts into the base of the distal phalanx of the big toe. The dorsalis pedis artery is palpated immediately lateral to its tendon on the dorsum of the foot. Weakness of great toe extension is a sensitive early sign of an L5 root lesion.
spotters.followup: Which root value is tested by resisted extension of the great toe, and what other muscle group would you test to confirm it?

spotters.prompt: Identify this muscle, give its nerve supply, and state where its tendon ends.
spotters.answer: Fibularis longus. Superficial fibular nerve, L5, S1 and S2. Arises from the head and upper two thirds of the lateral surface of the fibula, its tendon passes behind the lateral malleolus, then grooves the cuboid bone and crosses the sole obliquely to insert into the lateral side of the medial cuneiform bone and the base of the first metatarsal bone. Everts and plantar flexes the foot, and its sling across the sole is the main dynamic support of the transverse arch.
spotters.followup: Which muscle has an almost identical insertion approached from the opposite side, and what arch do the two together support?

spotters.prompt: Identify this artery and state how it reaches the compartment it lies in.
spotters.answer: Anterior tibial artery. Smaller terminal branch of the popliteal artery, arising at the lower border of popliteus and entering the anterior compartment through the oval gap in the upper part of the interosseous membrane of leg. It descends on the anterior surface of that membrane with the deep fibular nerve, lying between tibialis anterior and extensor hallucis longus in the lower leg, and becomes the dorsalis pedis artery at the front of the ankle midway between the malleoli.
spotters.followup: Name its recurrent branch at the knee and the anastomosis it enters.

spotters.prompt: Identify this artery and state exactly where you palpate it.
spotters.answer: Dorsalis pedis artery. Continuation of the anterior tibial artery distal to the ankle. Palpated on the dorsum of the foot lateral to the tendon of extensor hallucis longus, in the proximal part of the first intermetatarsal space, against the intermediate cuneiform bone. It passes between the two heads of the first dorsal interosseous muscle as the deep plantar artery to complete the plantar arch. Congenitally absent or aberrant in roughly one in twenty limbs, so absence alone is not proof of disease.
spotters.followup: Which artery does its deep plantar branch join in the sole, and what does that anastomosis form?

spotters.prompt: Identify this bone and state the vascular consequence of a fracture of its neck.
spotters.answer: Femur. Longest and strongest bone in the body. The head is supplied mainly by retinacular branches of the medial and lateral circumflex femoral arteries running along the neck under the retinacular fibres, with a small contribution from the artery of the ligamentum teres. An intracapsular fracture of the neck tears these retinacular vessels and commonly causes avascular necrosis of the head, which is why such fractures in the elderly are usually treated with replacement rather than fixation.
spotters.followup: Distinguish intracapsular from extracapsular neck fractures and explain why the prognosis differs.

spotters.prompt: Identify this bone and state the nerve injured at its upper end.
spotters.answer: Fibula. Non weight-bearing bone of the leg, providing muscle attachment and forming the lateral malleolus of the ankle mortise. The common fibular nerve winds around its neck, where it lies against bone with almost no soft tissue cover. Fracture of the neck, a tight plaster, or prolonged crossed-leg posture injures the nerve and produces foot drop with loss of dorsiflexion and eversion and sensory loss over the dorsum of the foot and lateral leg.
spotters.followup: Which muscles are paralysed in that lesion, and which single movement is preserved that distinguishes it from an L5 root lesion?

spotters.prompt: Identify this bone and name the shelf on its medial surface.
spotters.answer: Calcaneus. Largest and strongest tarsal bone, forming the heel and transmitting body weight to the ground. The sustentaculum tali projects medially from its upper part, supporting the talus above and grooved below by the tendon of flexor hallucis longus. Its posterior tuberosity gives insertion to the calcaneal tendon and origin to the first layer of the sole. A fall from a height drives the talus into it and causes a comminuted fracture, classically with an associated burst fracture of the lumbar spine.
spotters.followup: Which tendon grooves the undersurface of the sustentaculum tali, and which ligament attaches to its upper border?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned bone and state the commonest site of fracture in it.
spotters.answer: Clavicle. It is the only bony strut connecting the upper limb to the axial skeleton, articulating medially at the sternoclavicular joint and laterally at the acromioclavicular joint. The commonest fracture site is the junction of the middle and lateral thirds. The lateral fragment is pulled down by the weight of the limb and the medial fragment pulled up by sternocleidomastoid. It is the first bone in the body to ossify and the last to complete ossification.
spotters.followup: Which vessels and nerve trunk lie immediately deep to the middle third and are at risk in a displaced fracture, and which muscle protects them?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned muscle part and give its nerve supply and chief action.
spotters.answer: Acromial part of deltoid, the middle multipennate part arising from the acromion. Nerve supply is the axillary nerve (C5, C6). It is the main abductor of the arm from about 15 to 90 degrees, taking over from supraspinatus. Its multipennate architecture gives it power for this action.
spotters.followup: How would you test the axillary nerve clinically in a patient with a painful shoulder who cannot abduct?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned muscle part and give its nerve supply.
spotters.answer: Descending part of trapezius, the upper fibres running from the external occipital protuberance, ligamentum nuchae and upper cervical spines to the lateral third of the clavicle. Motor supply is the spinal accessory nerve (CN XI), with C3 and C4 carrying proprioception. It elevates the scapula and, with serratus anterior, rotates the glenoid cavity upwards.
spotters.followup: Where does this nerve lie superficially in the posterior triangle of the neck, and what deformity follows its division at that point?
spotters.sub: Upper limb, back and scapular region

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned muscle and state what is anatomically distinctive about its nerve supply.
spotters.answer: Coracobrachialis. It arises from the tip of the coracoid process and inserts on the middle of the medial surface of the humeral shaft. Nerve supply is the musculocutaneous nerve (C5, C6, C7), which characteristically pierces the substance of the muscle before running between biceps and brachialis. It flexes and adducts the arm and is the medial marker of the floor of the axilla.
spotters.followup: Into what cutaneous nerve does the musculocutaneous nerve continue, and where does it emerge?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned muscle. Give its nerve supply and its insertion.
spotters.answer: Brachialis. It arises from the lower half of the anterior surface of the humerus and inserts into the coronoid process and tuberosity of the ulna. Nerve supply is the musculocutaneous nerve (C5, C6), with the lateral part receiving a twig from the radial nerve. Because it inserts on the ulna it is the workhorse flexor of the elbow in every position of the forearm, unlike biceps whose power is greatest in supination.
spotters.followup: Which muscle forms the floor of the cubital fossa, and name the contents of that fossa from lateral to medial.

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned muscle. State its nerve supply and explain why its supply is exceptional for its action.
spotters.answer: Brachioradialis. It arises from the upper two thirds of the lateral supracondylar ridge of the humerus and inserts on the base of the styloid process of the radius. It is supplied by the radial nerve (C5, C6) yet it is a flexor of the elbow, which is exceptional because the radial nerve otherwise supplies extensors. It is most efficient with the forearm midprone and forms the lateral boundary of the cubital fossa.
spotters.followup: Which reflex tests the C5 and C6 segments through this muscle, and where do you strike to elicit it?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned muscle and name the condition affecting the compartment its tendon occupies.
spotters.answer: Abductor pollicis longus. It arises from the posterior surfaces of the ulna, radius and interosseous membrane and inserts on the base of the first metacarpal bone. Nerve supply is the posterior interosseous nerve (C7, C8). With extensor pollicis brevis it forms the anterior or lateral border of the anatomical snuffbox and shares the first extensor compartment, where stenosing tenovaginitis produces de Quervain disease, positive on the Finkelstein test.
spotters.followup: Name the boundaries, floor and contents of the anatomical snuffbox.

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned muscle and state its nerve supply and clinical importance.
spotters.answer: Abductor pollicis brevis. It arises from the flexor retinaculum and the tubercles of the scaphoid and trapezium and inserts into the lateral side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the thumb. Nerve supply is the recurrent branch of the median nerve (C8, T1). It abducts the thumb at right angles to the palm and is the muscle tested to confirm median nerve function, since wasting of the thenar eminence and loss of true thumb abduction are the cardinal motor signs of carpal tunnel syndrome.
spotters.followup: Why is sensation over the thenar eminence preserved in carpal tunnel syndrome but lost in a median nerve laceration higher in the forearm?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned artery and state where it begins and ends.
spotters.answer: Axillary artery. It is the continuation of the subclavian artery, beginning at the outer border of the first rib and ending at the lower border of teres major, where it becomes the brachial artery. It is divided into three parts by pectoralis minor and is enclosed with the cords of the brachial plexus in the axillary sheath, a prolongation of the prevertebral fascia.
spotters.followup: How are the cords of the brachial plexus arranged around the second part of this artery, and what is the scapular anastomosis?

competencies.statement: Describe the general features and functions of bones, and identify these features on bones of the upper limb.
competencies.note: Code AN1.1 and its subject (general features of bone) are reconstructed from memory of the NMC CBME 2019 Anatomy document, not quoted verbatim. My wording is a paraphrase. The topic heading 'General anatomy' is confident; the exact sub-number is high confidence but not quoted.

competencies.statement: Classify bones as long, short, flat, irregular, pneumatic and sesamoid, with examples from the upper limb.
competencies.note: Reconstructed from memory, not quoted. Pisiform is the sesamoid example and clavicle the atypical long bone; both exist in the model. No pneumatic bone exists in this block, so that class can only be named, not shown.

competencies.statement: Describe the blood supply of a long bone and the concept of nutrient and periosteal supply.
competencies.note: Code and wording reconstructed from memory. Honest limitation: the model has no named nutrient arteries or periosteum. This competency can only be demonstrated by pairing each long bone with the parent trunk from which its nutrient branch arises, which is an inference the teacher must state aloud.

competencies.statement: Explain the terms diaphysis, epiphysis, metaphysis, epiphyseal plate and growing end, and identify them on upper limb long bones.
competencies.note: Reconstructed from memory. I am moderately confident this sits at AN1.4 or AN1.5; departments using a different print should re-map the sub-number. The model geometry is adult bone, so the epiphyseal plate itself is not a separate mesh: regions are pointed out on the whole-bone mesh.

competencies.statement: Describe the classification of muscle by shape and fibre architecture and identify examples of each on the upper limb.
competencies.note: Code AN2.1 and the wording are reconstructed from memory, not quoted. Deltoid is the multipennate example and is present only as three named parts, which is actually convenient for teaching its three fibre directions.

competencies.statement: Describe the general structure of arteries and veins and distinguish them by wall, lumen and course on named upper limb vessels.
competencies.note: Code and wording reconstructed from memory. The model pairs venae comitantes with their arteries (radial artery and radial vein, ulnar artery and ulnar vein), which makes the artery versus vein contrast directly demonstrable.

competencies.statement: Explain the terms anastomosis, collateral circulation and end artery, and demonstrate arterial anastomoses of the upper limb.
competencies.note: Code and wording reconstructed from memory. This is the strongest general anatomy competency in this model: the elbow anastomosis is present as four named recurrent and collateral vessels plus both parent trunks, and the palmar arches are complete.

competencies.statement: Describe and demonstrate the attachments, nerve supply and actions of pectoralis major, pectoralis minor, serratus anterior and subclavius.
competencies.note: Code AN7.1 and the muscle list are reconstructed from memory of the CBME pectoral region topic, not quoted. Nerve supply cannot be shown: the model contains no pectoral, long thoracic or nerve to subclavius geometry, so that half of the competency is spoken, not pinned.

competencies.statement: Explain the anatomical basis of winging of the scapula.
competencies.note: The sub-number is uncertain: I am reconstructing this as AN7.5, and some prints place winging of scapula at AN7.6 or under the axilla topic. The long thoracic nerve is absent from the model, so the lesion is taught through the muscle and its scapular attachment, with the antagonist scapular retractors shown for contrast.

competencies.statement: Describe and identify the boundaries, walls and contents of the axilla.
competencies.note: Code AN8.1 and wording reconstructed from memory. Latissimus dorsi is absent from this model, so the posterior wall is incomplete and must be flagged to students. Axillary lymph nodes and the brachial plexus are also absent, so contents are limited to the vessels.

competencies.statement: Describe the extent, parts, relations and branches of the axillary artery.
competencies.note: Sub-number uncertain. I am reconstructing the axillary artery competency as AN8.2, but in some prints AN8.2 is the brachial plexus and the artery sits at AN8.3 or AN8.4. Departments should re-map against their own scheme. Note the model has no subscapular artery trunk or lateral thoracic artery: circumflex scapular artery is present without its parent, and the three-part division must be taught using pectoralis minor as the landmark.

competencies.statement: Describe and demonstrate the attachments, nerve supply and actions of the muscles connecting the upper limb to the vertebral column.
competencies.note: Code AN9.1 reconstructed from memory. Latissimus dorsi is absent from the model, which is a real gap in this competency and should be declared. Trapezius exists only as three named parts, which suits teaching its three actions on the scapula separately. Accessory nerve and dorsal scapular nerve are absent.

competencies.statement: Describe and demonstrate the attachments, nerve supply and actions of deltoid and the muscles of the rotator cuff.
competencies.note: Code AN10.1 reconstructed from memory. Structure names copied exactly, including the inconsistency in the model list where infraspinatus carries the word muscle and supraspinatus does not. All four cuff muscles are present, so this competency maps cleanly. Nerve supply is spoken only.

competencies.statement: Describe the arterial anastomosis around the scapula and explain its significance in obstruction of the axillary artery.
competencies.note: Sub-number reconstructed, likely AN10.2 or AN10.3. Wording is my paraphrase. All three limbs of the scapular anastomosis exist as separate meshes, which is unusual and makes this one of the best supported applied competencies in the block. The subscapular artery trunk itself is absent.

competencies.statement: Explain the anatomical basis of injury to the axillary nerve and the posterior circumflex humeral vessels in fracture of the surgical neck of the humerus and in shoulder dislocation.
competencies.note: Sub-number reconstructed and uncertain. The axillary nerve does not exist in this model, so the quadrangular space contents can only be shown as the posterior circumflex humeral artery plus the boundary muscles, with the nerve described verbally alongside its artery. Denervation is demonstrated on deltoid and teres minor.

competencies.statement: Describe and demonstrate the attachments, nerve supply and actions of the muscles of the anterior and posterior compartments of the arm.
competencies.note: Code AN11.1 reconstructed from memory. Serious and declarable gap: biceps brachii and triceps brachii are both absent from this model, so the two principal muscles of the competency cannot be shown. What remains is brachialis and coracobrachialis in front and anconeus behind. A department should treat this competency as only partially supported.

topics.topic: Male versus female bony pelvis: general build
topics.male_form: Heavier, thicker bones with rough, well marked muscle impressions. Ilium tall and set more vertically, iliac fossa deep. Whole pelvis is deep and narrow, built for weight transmission and locomotion in a heavier frame. Greater pelvis shallow relative to height of the ilium.
topics.female_form: Lighter, thinner, smoother bones with faint muscle markings. Ilium is lower and flared laterally, iliac fossa shallow, so the iliac crests lie further apart while the acetabula stay comparatively close. Whole pelvis is broad and shallow, built as a birth canal. Greater pelvis wide, giving the characteristic wider hip contour.
topics.why_examined: Question one of every general anatomy viva on the pelvis, and the anchor question in the pelvis chapter of BD Chaurasia and Cunningham's. Also the standard first year osteology spot.
topics.clinical: Anthropological and forensic sex determination of skeletal remains. Also underlies the wider female hip contour that governs gait mechanics and hip loading.
topics.exam_q: Q. Give four general differences between the male and the female pelvis as a whole. A. Female bones lighter and smoother with faint markings, ilium more flared and less vertical, pelvis broad and shallow rather than deep and narrow, greater pelvis wider with more widely separated iliac crests.

topics.topic: Pelvic inlet: heart shaped versus transversely oval
anchor_structures: intervertebral disk of fifth lumbar vertebra
topics.male_form: Inlet is heart shaped or cardiform because the sacral promontory projects forward strongly and indents the brim. Anteroposterior and transverse diameters are more nearly equal. Pelvic brim is rounded and blunt.
topics.female_form: Inlet is transversely oval or nearly circular, because the promontory is less prominent and the ilia are flared. Standard obstetric diameters: true or anatomical conjugate about 11 cm, transverse about 13 cm, oblique about 12 cm. The transverse diameter clearly exceeds the anteroposterior diameter.
topics.why_examined: Standard MBBS long answer, and the entry point for the obstetric pelvis in second year and in obstetrics. Numbers are asked directly.
topics.clinical: A contracted inlet with true conjugate under 10 cm predicts cephalopelvic disproportion and failure of the head to engage. Diagonal conjugate is measured clinically from the lower border of the pubic symphysis to the promontory, about 12.5 cm, and the obstetric conjugate is estimated by subtracting 1.5 to 2 cm.
topics.exam_q: Q. Name the diameters of the female pelvic inlet with their values, and state the shape of the inlet in each sex. A. Anteroposterior or true conjugate 11 cm, oblique 12 cm, transverse 13 cm. Male inlet is heart shaped, female inlet is transversely oval.

topics.topic: Subpubic angle and the pubic arch
topics.male_form: Subpubic angle is narrow, roughly 50 to 60 degrees, shaped like an inverted V. The ischiopubic rami are everted where the crura of the penis attach, and the arch is deep and narrow.
topics.female_form: Subpubic angle is wide, roughly 80 to 90 degrees, shaped like a rounded U. The rami are less everted and the arch is shallow and rounded, so the fetal head can occupy it as it extends under the symphysis.
topics.why_examined: The single most quoted difference in every Indian and Gulf MBBS paper, and the most reliable single visual trait in forensic sexing of the pelvis.
topics.clinical: A narrow subpubic arch reduces the effective outlet and forces the head posteriorly onto the perineum, increasing perineal tearing and the need for episiotomy. Assessed on clinical pelvimetry by admitting two fingers under the arch in the male pattern versus a fist across the intertuberous diameter in the female pattern.
topics.exam_q: Q. State the subpubic angle in each sex and its obstetric significance. A. Male about 50 to 60 degrees and V shaped, female about 80 to 90 degrees and U shaped. The wide female arch accommodates the fetal head during extension at the outlet.

topics.topic: Greater sciatic notch and ischial spines
topics.male_form: Greater sciatic notch is narrow and deep, subtending roughly 50 to 60 degrees, and admits about two fingers. Ischial spines are prominent and inverted, projecting into the pelvic cavity, so the interspinous diameter is reduced.
topics.female_form: Greater sciatic notch is wide and shallow, approaching a right angle, and admits about three fingers. Ischial spines are less prominent and everted, giving an interspinous diameter of about 10.5 cm, which is the narrowest plane of the whole female pelvis.
topics.why_examined: Asked as a paired difference in the pelvis long answer, and used in forensic anthropology because the notch survives fragmentation.
topics.clinical: The ischial spine is the landmark for transvaginal pudendal nerve block, the reference point for assessing fetal station in labour, station zero being at the spines, and the attachment of the sacrospinous ligament used in sacrospinous colpopexy for vault prolapse.
topics.exam_q: Q. How does the greater sciatic notch differ in the two sexes, and what is the clinical importance of the ischial spine? A. Narrow, about 50 to 60 degrees in the male, wide and near a right angle in the female. The spine gives fetal station zero, is the landmark for pudendal block, and anchors the sacrospinous ligament.

topics.topic: Sacrum: shape, promontory and auricular surface
topics.male_form: Sacrum is long, narrow and evenly curved through its length. The promontory is prominent and projects forward into the inlet. The auricular surface extends over about two and a half to three vertebrae. Sacral index, that is breadth over length times 100, is lower, of the order of 105.
topics.female_form: Sacrum is short, wide and set more vertically, the upper part relatively flat with the sharper curve confined to the lower part, which enlarges the cavity. The promontory is less prominent. The auricular surface extends over about two to two and a half vertebrae. Sacral index is higher, of the order of 115.
topics.why_examined: Part of the classic tabulated comparison, and separately examinable in vertebral column osteology and in forensic medicine.
topics.clinical: The promontory is the posterior landmark for the obstetric conjugate and is palpated on diagonal conjugate measurement. It is also the entry landmark for laparoscopic sacrocolpopexy, where the left common iliac vein lies dangerously close in the midline.
topics.exam_q: Q. Compare the male and female sacrum. A. Male: long, narrow, uniformly curved, prominent promontory, auricular surface over three vertebrae. Female: short, broad, upper part flat with lower curve, less prominent promontory, auricular surface over two to two and a half vertebrae.

topics.topic: Obturator foramen, acetabulum and the ischiopubic ramus
topics.male_form: Obturator foramen is large and oval. Acetabulum is large, about 50 to 52 mm in diameter, and faces laterally. Its diameter is greater than the distance from the anterior acetabular margin to the pubic symphysis. Body of the pubis is triangular and the ischiopubic ramus is everted with a rough crural attachment area.
topics.female_form: Obturator foramen is small and triangular. Acetabulum is smaller, about 44 to 46 mm, and faces more anterolaterally, which contributes to the greater bicondylar angle at the knee. Acetabular diameter approximately equals the distance from its anterior margin to the symphysis. Body of the pubis is square or rectangular, and the ischiopubic ramus is narrow with a sharp inferior edge, one of the Phenice traits.
topics.why_examined: Tabulated in the standard pelvis comparison and specifically asked in forensic medicine as part of pubic sexing.
topics.clinical: Phenice traits of the pubis, that is the ventral arc, the subpubic concavity and the sharp medial ischiopubic ramus, give roughly 95 percent accuracy in sex determination from a single bone. Acetabular orientation is relevant to hip dysplasia and to component positioning in arthroplasty.
topics.exam_q: Q. Name the three Phenice traits and state their value. A. Ventral arc, subpubic concavity, and the sharp medial aspect of the ischiopubic ramus, all present in the female pubis, giving about 95 percent accuracy in sex determination.

sexdiff.honest_limits:
Comparative text is not a female model, and no amount of authored content changes that. Say this to buyers in the first meeting, not the third.

WHAT THIS MODULE HONESTLY DELIVERS
1. Every topic here is anchored to structures verified present in derived.json. I checked each anchor name programmatically against entities[].k, so nothing in the anchor lists is invented.
2. The teaching act is real: the professor pins a structure the student can rotate, section and isolate, then reads the comparative text off the card. For roughly 60 percent of these topics, notably the pelvis, urethra, ureter, internal iliac artery, inguinal canal and all the forensic sexing cards, the male structure IS the object of study and the female difference is genuinely a verbal comparison even in Gray's and Chaurasia. For those, text plus a male mesh is close to the full teaching value.
3. The module covers the exam surface. Sex differences in gross anatomy are examined overwhelmingly as tabulated comparisons and viva questions, not as image identification, and 36 authored comparisons cover essentially all of it for MBBS and Gulf equivalents.

WHAT IT CANNOT DO
1. It cannot show a single female structure. Uterus, ovary, uterine tube, vagina, broad ligament, round ligament, uterine artery, clitoris, labia, bulb of vestibule and the female urethra are all absent. Where the card says "the female form is", the student sees nothing new on screen. A student cannot identify the pouch of Douglas in a spotter station because it is not there.
2. It cannot support a female spotter examination, a female sectional anatomy exercise, or any assessment item that requires the student to point at female geometry. The 614 existing spotter stations remain male only.
3. Several anchors are coarser than the teaching needs. The hip bone is a single fused mesh piece, so the ilium, ischium and pubis are not separately selectable and the pubic symphysis, ischial spine, ischial tuberosity, acetabular rim and greater sciatic notch can only be pointed at as surface features of one object, not isolated or measured as named parts. The Phenice traits and the subpubic angle are therefore demonstrated by rotating the hip bone, not by selecting the pubis.
4. The coccyx does not exist in this mesh. I searched all 2,234 mesh pieces: there is a sacrum and no coccyx. The coccyx appears in the authored card text only. Any card involving coccygeal retropulsion in labour, the sacrococcygeal joint or the anococcygeal ligament is taught against the sacrum with an explicit statement that the coccyx is missing.
5. Other absences hit specific cards: no peritoneum, so the rectovesical and rectouterine pouches are taught as the space between two pinned organs; no perineal body, no bulbospongiosus, no ischiocavernosus, no deep transverse perineal muscle, so the perineum card anchors on the external anal sphincter and levator ani only; no breast, no lymph nodes, so the breast card teaches the bed and the arteries and describes the gland; no heart as a whole organ and no thyroid gland, so those cards teach around a hole and should say so aloud; no peripheral nerves at all, so the pudendal nerve, which is the entire point of the ischial spine card, is described and never shown.
6. Confidence is not uniform. I marked 20 topics high, 16 medium, none low. Medium means either the numeric values vary between standard texts and populations (sacral index, acetabular diameter, gonial angle, carrying angle, femoral head cut offs, cranial capacity), or the claim rests on a specific study I am recalling rather than a settled textbook fact (three wedged lumbar vertebrae in women, sexually dimorphic hypothalamic nuclei), or modern evidence has weakened the classical teaching (appendix displacement in pregnancy, corpus callosum dimorphism, gonial angle discrimination). I did not verify any of this against a live source in this session: I had no network access and worked from memory of Gray's, Chaurasia, Cunningham's and Snell's. Every medium card should be checked against a current edition before a professor reads it to 150 students, and the forensic cut off values should be replaced with Indian and Gulf population standards where those exist, because most published cut offs derive from European skeletal series.

COMMERCIAL HONESTY
This module is worth building because it is fast, cheap, defensible and it makes the male mesh teach more than it currently does. It is not a substitute for female geometry and should never be sold as one. The correct positioning is: complete comparative sex differences content, taught against a male model, with the female model on the roadmap. A buyer who is told that up front will accept it. A buyer who discovers it in month two will not.
